cards.b: One parent, no fusion of gametes, no change in chromosome number. Offspring are genetically identical clones; only mutation creates variation.
Fusion of two haploid gametes to form a diploid zygote. Offspring get genetic material from two parents, so are genetically different.
Fusion of male and female gametes to form a diploid zygote, starting development of a new organism.
When the blastocyst adheres to and embeds in the endometrium (uterine wall), about day 7. Marks the start of pregnancy.
The ability to produce fertile offspring; the likelihood of an individual's genes being passed to the next generation.
The ongoing survival of a species as characteristics are passed from parents to offspring in a continuous lineage.
An egg develops into an embryo without fertilisation (e.g. some insects and reptiles).
An organism with both male and female reproductive organs; easier to reproduce but costs more energy to grow both sets.

cards.f: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction (variation, speed, energy).
cards.b: Asexual: one parent, mitosis, clones, fast, low energy, variation only by mutation. Sexual: two parents, meiosis plus fertilisation, unique offspring, slower, high energy, much more variation.

cards.f: Advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction?
cards.b: Adv: one parent, quick, rapid colonisation, favourable traits kept, energy efficient. Disadv: no variation, so poor adaptation to change or new disease; pathogens spread easily between identical individuals.

cards.f: Advantages and disadvantages of sexual reproduction?
cards.b: Adv: variation, so population can adapt and is less likely to be wiped out; drives evolution. Disadv: slow, needs a mate and energy, fewer offspring, may break up favourable gene combinations.

cards.f: How does each type of reproduction ensure continuity of a species?
cards.b: Asexual rapidly increases numbers in a stable environment. Sexual creates variation so some individuals survive environmental change and reproduce (natural selection).

External: gametes meet outside in water, huge gamete numbers, low fertilisation and survival, little parental care (staghorn coral). Internal: inside female tract, fewer eggs, high fertilisation, protected embryo, suits land (mammals).
Little energy per gamete, very many offspring, wide dispersal reduces competition, parents need not be together. Example: staghorn coral releasing millions of gametes, synchronised by pheromones.
Fertilisation much more likely, embryo protected, higher offspring survival, fewer gametes needed, allows reproduction on land. Example: mammals, birds, reptiles.

Oviparity: eggs laid, develop outside (birds, crocodiles, monotremes). Ovoviviparity: eggs hatch inside the mother, young born live (some snakes). Viviparity: embryo nourished directly inside the mother (placental mammals).

cards.f: Name the male and female parts of a flower.
cards.b: Male (stamen): anther (makes pollen), filament. Female (carpel/pistil): stigma (catches pollen), style (pollen tube grows down), ovary (becomes fruit), ovules (become seeds).
Self: pollen from the same flower/plant; less energy, less variation. Cross: pollen from another plant; more genetic diversity but needs agents (wind, water, insects, birds).

Wind: small dull unscented petals, no nectar, long hanging anthers, large feathery stigma, huge amounts of light pollen. Insect: large colourful scented petals, nectar, enclosed anthers, sticky pollen.

cards.f: Steps of double fertilisation in flowering plants?
cards.b: 1. Pollen lands on stigma. 2. Pollen tube grows down style. 3. Generative nucleus forms two sperm. 4. Tube enters ovule via micropyle. 5. One sperm + egg = zygote; other + two polar nuclei = triploid endosperm. 6. Ovule becomes seed. 7. Ovary becomes fruit.

cards.f: Name the methods of plant asexual reproduction with examples.
cards.b: Runners/stolons (strawberry), rhizomes (ginger, banana), tubers (potato), bulbs (onion), suckers (raspberry), apomixis (dandelion), fragmentation (mosses), cuttings and grafting (roses, fruit trees). All by mitosis.

cards.f: Is vegetative propagation by mitosis or meiosis?
cards.b: Mitosis (one source wrongly said meiosis). Offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
1. Nucleus divides by mitosis. 2. A bud bulges from the parent cell. 3. Cytokinesis when the bud is nearly parent size. 4. Bud detaches (or stays attached in a chain) and grows independently.

cards.f: How do fungi reproduce by spores?
cards.b: Hyphae (mycelium) spread through food; sporangia release haploid spores made by mitosis; spores dispersed by wind, water or animals; germinate in moist conditions into a new mycelium. Examples: bread mould, Penicillium.

cards.f: Steps of sexual reproduction in fungi?
cards.b: 1. Compatible haploid mycelia touch. 2. Plasmogamy: cytoplasm fuses, two nuclei in one cell. 3. Karyogamy: nuclei fuse into a diploid nucleus. 4. Meiosis produces varied haploid spores, often in a fruiting body.

cards.f: Steps of binary fission in bacteria?
cards.b: 1. Cell elongates. 2. Circular chromosome replicates, copies attached to membrane. 3. Plasmids replicate. 4. Chromosomes move to opposite poles. 5. Membrane and wall grow inwards. 6. Cell splits into two identical clones.

cards.f: Is bacterial binary fission sexual or asexual?
cards.b: Asexual (one source wrongly labelled it sexual). Like mitosis but with no spindle or nucleus; E. coli can divide every 20 minutes.

cards.f: How do bacteria gain variation without sexual reproduction?
cards.b: High mutation rates and horizontal gene transfer: conjugation (plasmid through a pilus), transformation (naked DNA taken up), transduction (bacteriophage carries DNA).

Asexual: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium) and budding. Sexual: syngamy (two haploid cells fuse) or conjugation (Paramecium exchanges micronuclei). Plasmodium shows fast reproduction aids disease spread.

cards.f: Compare placental mammals, marsupials and monotremes.
cards.b: Placental: long gestation nourished by placenta (humans). Marsupials: simple short-lived placenta, undeveloped young finish in pouch (kangaroo). Monotremes: lay eggs, young suckle from skin pores (echidna, platypus).

cards.f: Where are FSH and LH made, and what makes GnRH?
cards.b: FSH and LH: anterior pituitary. GnRH: hypothalamus (one source wrongly said gonadotropins are made in the hypothalamus).

GnRH (hypothalamus) → FSH and LH (anterior pituitary). FSH stimulates sperm production. LH stimulates Leydig cells to release testosterone, which drives spermatogenesis and secondary sex characteristics.
No sperm in semen. (A low sperm count is oligospermia.)

1. Follicular (days 1–13): FSH grows follicles, which secrete oestrogen; endometrium thickens. 2. Ovulation (~day 14): high oestrogen → LH surge → egg released. 3. Luteal (15–28): corpus luteum secretes progesterone. 4. No fertilisation: corpus luteum degenerates, menstruation.
High oestrogen from the dominant follicle switches to positive feedback, causing an LH surge; the LH surge triggers ovulation. Oestrogen does not trigger it directly.
The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and some oestrogen to maintain the endometrium. Without hCG it degenerates, hormones fall, menstruation begins.

cards.f: Compare negative and positive feedback in reproduction.
cards.b: Negative counteracts change (progesterone and oestrogen inhibit GnRH, FSH, LH in the luteal phase). Positive amplifies change (LH surge; oxytocin in childbirth).

1. Ovulation. 2. Sperm ejaculated. 3. Sperm swim to fallopian tube. 4. Penetrate corona radiata. 5. Acrosome reaction digests zona pellucida. 6. Membranes fuse. 7. Cortical reaction blocks polyspermy. 8. Haploid nuclei fuse → diploid zygote (46).
When the sperm head binds zona pellucida glycoproteins, the acrosome releases digestive enzymes that digest a path through it.
Block to polyspermy: cortical granules in the egg release enzymes that harden the zona pellucida so no other sperm can enter.

1. Day 0–1: fertilisation in fallopian tube. 2. Day 2: cleavage. 3. Day 3–4: morula. 4. Day 4–7: blastocyst (trophoblast forms placenta, inner cell mass forms embryo). 5. ~Day 7: implants in endometrium.

cards.f: Steps of hormonal control of pregnancy?
cards.b: 1. Trophoblast secretes hCG. 2. hCG maintains corpus luteum → progesterone and oestrogen. 3. These inhibit GnRH, FSH, LH (no ovulation). 4. By week 10–12 placenta takes over progesterone and oestrogen. 5. Prolactin rises from trimester 2.
Secreted by trophoblast/placenta; maintains the corpus luteum so it keeps making progesterone and oestrogen in early pregnancy. Detected by pregnancy tests.
Maintains and vascularises the endometrium, prevents uterine contractions, inhibits FSH and LH, develops mammary glands. Milk production itself is driven by prolactin, not progesterone.

cards.f: Steps of hormonal control of birth?
cards.b: 1. Foetal stress → foetal ACTH → cortisol. 2. Cortisol lowers progesterone, raises oestrogen. 3. Oestrogen adds oxytocin receptors, prostaglandins released. 4. Head presses cervix → stretch receptors → hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases oxytocin. 5. Stronger contractions → more oxytocin until birth.

cards.f: Why is birth a positive feedback loop?
cards.b: Contractions stretch the cervix, stretch receptors signal more oxytocin release, causing stronger contractions and more stretching, until the baby is born.

cards.f: Where is oxytocin made and released, and what does it do?
cards.b: Made in the hypothalamus, stored and released by the posterior pituitary. Causes labour contractions, milk let-down and maternal bonding.
From the anterior pituitary: milk production (rises from trimester 2), mammary gland enlargement, maternal behaviour.

cards.f: Role of relaxin and prostaglandins in birth?
cards.b: Relaxin softens the cervix and relaxes ligaments. Prostaglandins initiate labour, soften the cervix, sensitise the uterus to oxytocin and help expel the placenta.
Mother to foetus: O₂, glucose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins, antibodies. Foetus to mother: CO₂, urea, wastes. Bloods do not mix. Adaptations: chorionic villi, thin membranes, rich blood supply.

cards.f: Steps of artificial insemination (AI) in cattle?
cards.b: 1. Collect semen from a superior bull. 2. Check, dilute with extender, freeze in straws in liquid nitrogen (−196 °C). 3. Synchronise female oestrus. 4. Thaw and deposit just past the cervix with an AI gun.

cards.f: Advantages and disadvantages of artificial insemination?
cards.b: Adv: spreads superior genetics fast and worldwide, cheap access to elite bulls, synchronised births, no bulls needed. Disadv: needs skill and equipment, can harm females, reduces genetic diversity.
1. Emasculation: remove stamens before the flower opens. 2. Bag the flower. 3. Brush pollen from the chosen male parent onto the receptive stigma. 4. Rebag and tag to record the cross.

cards.f: Advantages and disadvantages of artificial pollination?
cards.b: Adv: concentrates desired traits, ensures pollination, increases yield. Disadv: time-consuming, reduces genetic diversity.
Hormones (prostaglandins, progesterone CIDR inserts, GnRH) bring a herd into oestrus within a narrow window for AI, giving uniform calving and group management.
A Holstein bull (not a cow) whose semen sired over 200,000 daughters via AI and earned about $25 million, spreading milk genes worldwide but reducing genetic diversity. Cloned in 2000.

cards.f: Exam structure: Evaluate the impact of scientific knowledge on manipulating reproduction in agriculture (7 marks).
cards.b: Judgement first. Describe AI (with Starbuck) and artificial pollination steps. Give a positive (yield, desirable traits, worldwide genetics) and negative (reduced diversity, monocultures, cost) for each. Restate the judgement.

cards.f: Describe the Watson and Crick model of DNA.
cards.b: Double helix of two antiparallel strands. Nucleotide = phosphate + deoxyribose + base. Sugar-phosphate backbone joined by covalent phosphodiester bonds; bases paired by hydrogen bonds (A–T two, G–C three).

cards.f: What are the complementary base pairs in DNA?
cards.b: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds). A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. (In RNA, A pairs with U.)
Covalent phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone; weak hydrogen bonds between bases (not covalent), allowing the strands to unzip.

cards.f: Which bases are purines and which are pyrimidines?
cards.b: Purines (double ring): adenine, guanine. Pyrimidines (single ring): thymine, cytosine, and uracil in RNA.

Chromatid: one of two identical copies of a replicated chromosome. Homologous chromosomes: a pair with the same genes in the same order, one from each parent. Karyotype: image of a full set of chromosomes in pairs.

1. Initiation at origins. 2. Helicase unwinds and breaks H bonds (replication fork). 3. Primase adds RNA primer. 4. DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides 5'→3' (leading continuous, lagging in Okazaki fragments). 5. Primers replaced. 6. Ligase joins fragments. 7. Proofreading. 8. Termination.
Each new DNA molecule contains one original parent strand and one newly made strand.

cards.f: Roles of helicase, primase, DNA polymerase and ligase?
cards.b: Helicase: unwinds, breaks H bonds. Primase: makes RNA primer. DNA polymerase: adds nucleotides 5'→3' and proofreads. Ligase: joins Okazaki fragments, seals backbone.

cards.f: Compare the leading and lagging strand.
cards.b: Leading: made continuously towards the fork. Lagging: made discontinuously in short Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer, later joined by ligase.
Interphase: G1 (growth, organelles duplicate), S (DNA replicates: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids), G2 (growth, error checking). Then M phase: mitosis and cytokinesis. G0 = non-dividing (nerve cells).

cards.f: How many chromatids in a human cell after S phase?
cards.b: 92 (46 chromosomes × 2 sister chromatids). One source wrongly said 96.

1. Prophase: chromosomes condense, spindle forms. 2. Prometaphase: nuclear envelope breaks down, spindle attaches. 3. Metaphase: chromosomes line up single file on equator. 4. Anaphase: sister chromatids pulled to poles. 5. Telophase: nuclei reform. 6. Cytokinesis.

cards.f: Do homologous chromosomes pair in mitosis?
cards.b: No. Homologues pair (synapsis) only in prophase I of meiosis.

cards.f: Compare cytokinesis in animal and plant cells.
cards.b: Animal: contractile ring pinches the membrane inwards (cleavage furrow). Plant: cell plate forms at the equator and cellulose is laid down to make a new wall.

1. Prophase I: homologues pair, crossing over. 2. Metaphase I: pairs line up randomly (independent assortment). 3. Anaphase I: homologues separate. 4. Telophase I: two haploid cells. 5. Meiosis II like mitosis: sister chromatids separate. Result: four unique haploid gametes.

cards.f: Are cells after telophase I haploid or diploid?
cards.b: Haploid (one chromosome of each pair, still as two chromatids). One source wrongly said diploid.

Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells, no pairing or crossing over, growth and repair. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 unique haploid gametes, synapsis and crossing over in prophase I. Both replicate DNA once and use a spindle.
So the zygote has the normal diploid number. Diploid gametes would double the chromosome number each generation (46 → 92 → 184).
Growth, repair and replacement of cells, asexual reproduction, and genetic stability (identical information in every cell).

cards.f: Calc: 2n = 8. Chromosomes and chromatids at metaphase of mitosis, metaphase I and metaphase II?
cards.b: Mitosis: 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids. Metaphase I: 8 (4 pairs), 16 chromatids. Metaphase II: 4 chromosomes, 8 chromatids per cell. Gamete combinations 2⁴ = 16.

cards.f: How many gamete combinations from independent assortment in humans?
cards.b: 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million per person. With random fertilisation, about 70 trillion possible children per couple, before crossing over.

cards.f: Exam structure: Assess the effect of cell replication on the continuity of species.
cards.b: Accurate DNA replication gives genetic stability. Mitosis allows growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis halves chromosome number and adds variation. Errors cause mutations or nondisjunction. Judgement: both stability and some variation are essential.

cards.f: Compare DNA in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
cards.b: Prokaryotes: single circular chromosome in nucleoid, no histones, plasmids, no introns or telomeres. Eukaryotes: linear chromosomes in nucleus wound on histones, introns, telomeres, plus mtDNA. Both double-stranded helices with the same 4 bases.

cards.f: Is prokaryotic DNA a double helix?
cards.b: Yes: a circular, double-stranded double helix (one source wrongly said it was not).

cards.f: What fraction of the human genome codes for protein?
cards.b: About 1–2%. Coding regions are exons; introns are one type of non-coding DNA.
Small, circular, double-stranded; replicates independently; inherited only from the mother; mutates about 10 times faster than nuclear DNA. Used to trace maternal ancestry.
Small circular DNA in prokaryotes coding for non-essential but useful proteins (e.g. antibiotic resistance); replicates independently and can be transferred.
DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose, A T G C, stable, long-term storage. RNA: usually single-stranded, ribose, A U G C, short-lived, gene expression.
mRNA: copy of a gene carrying codons to ribosomes. tRNA: cloverleaf with anticodon and specific amino acid. rRNA: made in nucleolus, forms ribosomes with proteins.
Codon: 3 mRNA bases coding one amino acid. Anticodon: 3 complementary bases on tRNA (codon UUA pairs with anticodon AAU).

cards.f: Key facts about the genetic code?
cards.b: 64 codons for 20 amino acids (redundant, so some mutations are silent). Start codon AUG (methionine). Stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA. Universal, so transgenic organisms are possible.

1. RNA polymerase binds the promoter. 2. RNA polymerase unwinds DNA (not helicase). 3. Reads template strand 3'→5'; RNA nucleotides pair (A–U). 4. Joins nucleotides. 5. Stops at terminator sequence. 6. Splicing removes introns; cap and poly-A tail added. 7. mRNA exits nucleus.

cards.f: What ends transcription and what ends translation?
cards.b: Transcription ends at a terminator sequence. Translation ends at a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA).

1. mRNA binds small ribosomal subunit; tRNA (anticodon UAC) brings methionine to AUG. 2. Next tRNA brings its amino acid. 3. Peptide bond forms. 4. Ribosome moves one codon; empty tRNA leaves. 5. Chain grows. 6. Stop codon releases polypeptide. 7. Folding and modification.

cards.f: Importance of mRNA in polypeptide synthesis?
cards.b: Carries a copy of one gene from the protected nucleus to ribosomes; codon order sets amino acid order; short-lived, so the cell can quickly adjust protein production; splicing allows several proteins per gene.

cards.f: Importance of tRNA in polypeptide synthesis?
cards.b: Adapter molecule: delivers specific amino acids and its anticodon matches the codon, ensuring the correct amino acid is placed. Without tRNA the code could not be translated.

cards.f: Calc: DNA template TAC AAA GGC ATT. mRNA and amino acids?
cards.b: mRNA AUG UUU CCG UAA: Met, Phe, Pro, stop.

cards.f: Describe the four levels of protein structure.
cards.b: Primary: amino acid sequence (peptide bonds). Secondary: alpha helices and beta sheets (H bonds). Tertiary: 3D shape from R group interactions, forms active site. Quaternary: two or more polypeptides (haemoglobin has 4).
Heat, extreme pH or chemicals disrupt bonds, destroying protein shape and function; often irreversible.
Fibrous: long, insoluble, structural (collagen, keratin). Globular: compact, soluble, functional (enzymes, antibodies, haemoglobin, hormones).

Enzymes (DNA polymerase), structural (collagen, keratin), contractile (actin, myosin), transport (haemoglobin), hormones (insulin), receptors, regulatory (p53), defence (antibodies), sensory (opsins).
Genotype: the alleles an organism carries. Phenotype: observable traits. Phenotype = genotype + environment.

Crocodile sex set by incubation temperature; hydrangeas blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline; Siamese cats darker in cool extremities; Arctic fox coat changes with season; human height and nutrition.
Chemical changes to DNA or histones that alter gene expression without changing the base sequence. Methylation silences genes; histone acetylation loosens chromatin and increases expression.

cards.f: How do epigenetics explain differences in identical twins?
cards.b: Twins share DNA but their epigenomes diverge with diet, stress, chemicals and experiences, changing gene expression and disease risk.

cards.f: Exam structure: Assess how genes and environment affect phenotypic expression.
cards.b: Genotype sets potential; environment modifies it (hydrangea, crocodile, Siamese cat); epigenetics links them (methylation, acetylation, twins). Judgement: phenotype results from the interaction of both.
Gene: DNA section coding for a polypeptide or functional RNA. Allele: alternative form of a gene. Locus: position of a gene on a chromosome.
Homozygous: two identical alleles (AA, aa). Heterozygous: two different (Aa). Carrier: heterozygote with a hidden recessive allele that can be passed on.
A trait controlled by many genes with small additive effects plus environment, giving continuous variation (height, skin colour, eye colour).

cards.f: How does crossing over create variation?
cards.b: In prophase I, non-sister chromatids of homologues break at chiasmata and swap segments, producing recombinant chromatids with new allele combinations; can separate linked genes.

cards.f: Compare independent assortment and random segregation.
cards.b: Independent assortment: random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I. Random segregation: alleles separate into different gametes at anaphase, each gamete gets one allele.

cards.f: What is the only source of brand-new alleles?
cards.b: Mutation. Crossing over, assortment and fertilisation only reshuffle existing alleles.
Segregation: two alleles per trait separate so each gamete carries one. Independent assortment: alleles of genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently.
1. Define a key (capital = dominant). 2. Write parent genotypes. 3. Separate each parent's gametes. 4. Draw grid. 5. Fill boxes. 6. State genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
Genotypic 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. Phenotypic 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
Cross a dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring → it was homozygous; about 50:50 → heterozygous.
Incomplete: heterozygote is a blend (red × white snapdragons → pink). Codominance: both alleles shown separately (roan cattle, AB blood). Both give 1:2:1 in F2. Treat them as distinct.
Multiple alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i. Iᴬ and Iᴮ codominant, both dominant to i. 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes. AB universal recipient; O universal donor.

cards.f: Calc: AB × AO (IᴬIᴮ × Iᴬi). Phenotype ratio?
cards.b: 2 A : 1 AB : 1 B. Genotypes IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi.

cards.f: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
cards.b: Males (XY) have one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed; they cannot be carriers. Females need two recessive alleles. Examples: haemophilia, red-green colour blindness, Duchenne MD.

cards.f: Calc: Carrier mother × normal father for haemophilia (XᴴXʰ × XᴴY)?
cards.b: 25% normal girl, 25% carrier girl, 25% normal boy, 25% affected boy. Half of sons affected; no daughters affected.

cards.f: Key rules of X-linked recessive inheritance?
cards.b: Mostly males; can skip generations; affected mother → all sons affected; affected daughter must have an affected father; father never passes it to a son.

cards.f: Why are tortoiseshell cats almost always female?
cards.b: Black (Xᴮ) and orange (Xᴼ) alleles are X-linked and codominant; tortoiseshell needs XᴮXᴼ, so two X chromosomes.

cards.f: Phenotype ratio of a dihybrid cross HhSs × HhSs?
cards.b: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (for unlinked genes). A dihybrid test cross with hhss gives 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Circle = female, square = male, shaded = affected, half-shaded = carrier. Horizontal line = mating; vertical = descent. Generations in Roman numerals.

1. Find parents with the same phenotype whose child differs. 2. Unaffected parents, affected child → recessive. 3. Affected parents, unaffected child → dominant. 4. Test sex linkage (affected daughter with unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive). 5. Prove with a Punnett square.

cards.f: Exam structure: Determine the mode of inheritance from a pedigree.
cards.b: State the pattern, cite individuals: 'Recessive because unaffected parents X and Y have affected child Z, so both are carriers (Aa × Aa).' Rule out X-linked: 'affected female has unaffected father'. Show Punnett square.

cards.f: How do you calculate allele frequency?
cards.b: Count alleles, not people: frequency of G = copies of G ÷ total copies of the gene. E.g. 36 GG, 48 Gg, 16 gg: G = (72 + 48) ÷ 200 = 0.60.

cards.f: State the Hardy-Weinberg equations and conditions.
cards.b: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Conditions: large population, random mating, no migration, no mutation, no natural selection.

cards.f: Calc: 45 of 500 show a recessive trait. Allele frequencies and carriers?

cards.b: A single nucleotide polymorphism: variation at one base position occurring in at least 1% of the population (under 1% = point mutation). Most common human variation (~90%).
Synonymous: no amino acid change (silent). Non-synonymous: changes the amino acid (sickle cell: glutamic acid → valine in beta-globin).
Markers to locate disease genes, GWAS association studies, pharmacogenomics, ancestry, evolutionary relatedness, forensics, polygenic risk scores.
Usually bi-allelic (less informative than STRs), only partly explain polygenic traits, may miss rare variants, European bias in studies, association is not causation.
Haplotype: group of tightly linked alleles/SNPs inherited together from one parent. Haplogroup: group of similar haplotypes sharing a common ancestral SNP.

1. Prepare/copy DNA. 2. Mix template, primer, polymerase, dNTPs and fluorescent ddNTPs. 3. Heat ~96 °C to denature. 4. Cool ~50 °C to anneal. 5. ~60 °C extend until a ddNTP stops the chain. 6. Repeat. 7. Capillary electrophoresis by size. 8. Laser reads colours shortest to longest.

cards.f: Why does a ddNTP stop chain growth?
cards.b: It lacks the 3' OH group, so no further nucleotide can attach.
Evolutionary and family relationships, species identification, detecting mutations (BRCA1/2), pathogen strains (COVID-19), personalised medicine, forensics.

cards.f: Facts about the Human Genome Project?
cards.b: Completed 2003, about two decades, ~US$3 billion; mapped ~3 billion base pairs and ~20,000–21,000 genes; located genes for over 4,000 disorders.

cards.f: Define: DNA profiling and who developed it.
cards.b: Comparing highly variable DNA regions (STRs) to produce a profile unique to each person except identical twins. Developed by Alec Jeffreys, University of Leicester, 1985.
Short tandem repeat: non-coding DNA where a 2–5 base sequence (e.g. GATA) repeats; repeat number varies between people. Two alleles per locus, one from each parent.

1. Collect sample. 2. Extract DNA. 3. Amplify STR loci by PCR with fluorescent primers. 4. Separate by gel or capillary electrophoresis. 5. Visualise (electropherogram). 6. Compare patterns. Cutting with restriction enzymes is the older RFLP method.
Forensics (link or exclude suspects), paternity testing (every child band matches mother or father), identifying victims, wildlife conservation and anti-poaching, genealogy.
Unwanted knowledge of late-onset disease (Huntington's), insurance discrimination, privacy of DNA databases, unclear ownership of genetic information, gene patents.

1. Agarose gel, wells at negative end. 2. Cut/amplify DNA, add loading dye. 3. Load samples and a DNA ladder. 4. Apply current: DNA moves to positive. 5. Small fragments travel further. 6. Stain and view under UV. 7. Compare with ladder.

cards.f: Why does DNA move towards the positive electrode?
cards.b: DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate groups. The gel acts as a sieve so smaller fragments move faster.

mtDNA haplotypes from wild koala tissue samples showed the southern lineage has the lowest genetic diversity; habitat fragmentation restricts gene flow. Guides conservation planning and immune gene research.

cards.f: Case study: red cardinals in Brazil.
cards.b: Microsatellite analysis found three genetic groups matching geography; seized trafficked birds matched one group, identifying hotspots and guiding release to native populations.

cards.f: Case study: woolly mammoth on Wrangel Island.
cards.b: The last population lost diversity through inbreeding, accumulating harmful mutations and disease susceptibility before extinction: a warning for conservation.

cards.f: What does the BRCA data show (trend and limitation)?
cards.b: African (15.6%) and Latin American highest totals, Middle Eastern lowest (9.4%); BRCA1 usually above BRCA2. Limitation: very uneven samples (36,235 vs 492) and European bias.

cards.f: What is a polygenic risk score (breast cancer)?
cards.b: 300+ SNPs each with tiny effects combined into one score from a blood test; with mammographic density and family history it improves risk prediction for personalised screening.

cards.f: What is the International HapMap Project?
cards.b: Worldwide collaboration mapping common haplotypes and SNP frequencies across populations to find variants linked to common diseases and trace lineages.

cards.f: Compare the Multiregional and Out of Africa (Replacement) hypotheses.
cards.b: Multiregional: H. erectus evolved into modern humans in parallel regions with gene flow (mostly fossil evidence; not supported). Out of Africa: H. sapiens left Africa and replaced archaic groups with limited interbreeding (mtDNA, Y evidence; favoured).

cards.f: What genetic evidence supports an African origin?
cards.b: Greatest genetic diversity is in African populations; non-Africans carry a subset. Diversity is greater within than between populations.
About 300,000 years ago from fossils; about 200,000 years from mtDNA estimates. Some interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

cards.f: Key genetic facts about migration to Australia?
cards.b: Sahul (Australia + New Guinea) joined until ~8,000 years ago. Madjedbebe rock shelter: occupation ~65,000 years. Denisovan DNA in Aboriginal Australians and Melanesians. Earliest major sea crossing.

cards.f: Can population genetic patterns be predicted accurately?
cards.b: Partly: Punnett squares and Hardy-Weinberg give good probabilities in large random-mating populations, and big data (HGP, HapMap) improves precision. But selection, drift, gene flow, polygenic traits and sample bias limit accuracy; predictions are probabilities.
A permanent change in the nucleotide sequence of an organism's DNA (or RNA in some viruses), if not fixed by DNA repair. Effects can be neutral, harmful or helpful.
Mutagen: an agent that causes (induces) mutations. Mutagenesis: the process of inducing a mutation.
Spontaneous: occurs naturally without an outside agent (DNA replication error, nondisjunction). Induced: caused by exposure to an external mutagen (radiation, chemicals, viruses).
1. Change in DNA 2. Change in mRNA 3. Change in amino acid sequence 4. Altered or non-functional protein 5. Altered phenotype.

1. Origin (spontaneous/induced) 2. Amount of DNA (point/chromosomal) 3. Effect on DNA (substitution, insertion, deletion) 4. Effect on phenotype (silent, neutral, helpful, harmful) 5. Heritability (somatic/germline).

Base excision repair (damaged base removed and replaced); mismatch repair ('spell check' of new DNA, plus polymerase proofreading); nucleotide excision repair (removes bulky damage such as thymine dimers).

cards.f: How does UV radiation cause mutation?
cards.b: Non-ionising. Adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand (most often T-T) bond covalently, forming a pyrimidine (thymine) dimer. This kinks the helix and stalls DNA/RNA polymerase, so wrong bases are inserted or replication stops. Causes skin cancers (melanoma).

cards.f: How does ionising radiation cause mutation?
cards.b: X-rays, gamma rays and cosmic rays remove electrons, forming ions and free radicals that break the sugar-phosphate backbone (single- and double-strand breaks). Wrongly rejoined breaks cause chromosomal mutations. Linked to leukaemia.

cards.f: What's the trap with UV vs ionising radiation?
cards.b: UV forms pyrimidine (thymine) dimers; it is mostly non-ionising. Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma) forms free radicals and strand breaks. Dimers form between adjacent pyrimidines (T-T, C-T, C-C), not 'thymine and cytosine' only.

cards.f: Which parts of the EM spectrum are mutagenic?
cards.b: Only the short-wavelength, high-energy end: UV, X-rays and gamma rays. Infrared and visible light are not.

cards.f: How do base analogues cause mutation?
cards.b: Chemicals similar to normal bases are incorporated during replication but pair incorrectly, causing substitutions in later rounds. E.g. 5-bromouracil acts like thymine but can pair with guanine.

cards.f: How do intercalating agents cause mutation?
cards.b: Flat molecules slip between stacked base pairs, distorting the helix and causing insertions or deletions (frameshifts) during replication; also inhibit polymerases. E.g. ethidium bromide.

cards.f: How do base-modifying chemicals and heavy metals cause mutation?
cards.b: Base modifiers (tobacco nitrosamines, benzene, aflatoxin) alter bases causing mispairing, adducts and breaks. Heavy metals (arsenic, nickel, cobalt) interfere with DNA repair and replication fidelity.

cards.f: Agent Orange: what does it show?
cards.b: A Vietnam War herbicide contaminated with TCDD (dioxin), a mutagen and carcinogen. Linked to cancers, birth defects and miscarriages; shows long-lasting, intergenerational (germ-line) effects of mutagens.

cards.f: How do viruses act as mutagens?
cards.b: Insert their genetic material into host chromosomes (insertional mutagenesis), disrupting genes or their regulation, e.g. switching on oncogenes. HPV → cervical cancer; HIV; hepatitis B.

cards.f: How do bacteria act as mutagens?
cards.b: Infections cause chronic inflammation, producing reactive molecules and reducing DNA repair efficiency. Helicobacter pylori is linked to stomach cancer.
DNA segments that cut or copy themselves and insert at new positions, disrupting genes or altering expression. Discovered by Barbara McClintock in maize (variegated kernels).

Natural chemicals: pyrrolizidine alkaloids (plants), aflatoxin (mould), cycasin (cycads), free radicals from metabolism, nitrosamines formed from dietary nitrites. Natural radiation: cosmic rays, radon.
A change in a single (or a few) nucleotide base pairs at a specific locus within one gene. Caused by replication errors, mutagens or repair failure.
The same type of change is a point mutation if fewer than 1% of the population carry it, and an SNP if 1% or more do.
Substitution (one base swapped; most common; one codon affected), insertion (extra bases added), deletion (bases removed). Insertions and deletions cause frameshifts unless a multiple of 3.
The new codon codes for the same amino acid (genetic code is redundant, e.g. GCC→GCA both alanine) or the change is in non-coding DNA; no change to the polypeptide.

A codon changes to code for a different amino acid. Sickle cell anaemia: A→T substitution in the beta-globin gene changes GAG to GTG, so glutamic acid becomes valine; haemoglobin crystallises and red cells sickle.
A codon changes to a premature stop codon, giving a truncated, usually non-functional protein. E.g. some forms of cystic fibrosis and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
An insertion or deletion (not a multiple of 3) shifts the reading frame so every later codon changes, often with an early stop. E.g. Tay-Sachs disease (4-base insertion).

cards.f: What's the trap with insertions and deletions?
cards.b: An indel of exactly 3 bases (or a multiple) does NOT shift the frame: it adds or removes one amino acid. E.g. CF allele F508del removes 3 bases, deleting one phenylalanine.
A change to the structure of a large chromosome segment (many genes) or to chromosome number.
Errors in crossing over (prophase I), nondisjunction in anaphase, breakage by ionising radiation or chemicals with incorrect rejoining; maternal age raises nondisjunction risk.
Deletion: ABEF. Duplication: ABCBCDEF. Inversion: ADCBEF. Translocation: segment moves to a NON-homologous chromosome (ABCPQR + MNODEF).
Deletion: cri-du-chat (part of chromosome 5 lost). Translocation: Philadelphia chromosome (9;22) in chronic myeloid leukaemia. Duplication: raw material for new genes in evolution.
Translocation moves a segment to a NON-homologous chromosome, not 'the other homologous chromosome'.
Gain or loss of one or a few whole chromosomes, caused by nondisjunction. Trisomy (2n+1): Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Klinefelter (47, XXY). Monosomy (2n−1): Turner syndrome (45, X0).

More than two complete SETS of chromosomes (3n, 4n...), from complete nondisjunction or failed cytokinesis. Common in plants: bread wheat (6n), strawberries (8n), seedless bananas (3n), potatoes (4n).

cards.f: What's the trap with trisomy and polyploidy?
cards.b: Trisomy (2n+1) and monosomy (2n−1) are aneuploidy, not polyploidy. Polyploidy means extra complete sets of chromosomes.
Failure of homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) to separate in anaphase, giving gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers and an aneuploid zygote.

cards.f: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs meiosis II: gamete outcome?
cards.b: Meiosis I: ALL four gametes abnormal (two n+1, two n−1). Meiosis II: HALF abnormal (one n+1, one n−1) and two normal.

cards.f: Why does maternal age increase nondisjunction risk?
cards.b: Oocytes begin meiosis before birth and are arrested in prophase I until ovulation, possibly for decades; the longer the wait, the higher the chance of error.

Point: one or few bases in one gene; replication errors/mutagens; often small or silent effects; detected by sequencing (sickle cell). Chromosomal: many genes or whole chromosomes; crossing-over errors/nondisjunction; large effects; detected by karyotype (Down syndrome). Both create variation.

Somatic: body cell, affects only that cell's mitotic descendants, not inherited, no evolutionary significance (melanoma, lung cancer). Germ-line: gamete, every cell of offspring, inherited, adds new alleles to the gene pool (cystic fibrosis, trisomy 21).

cards.f: Does a germ-line mutation affect the parent?
cards.b: No. It has no effect on the parent; it affects the offspring (all its cells) and their descendants.

cards.f: Can somatic mutations be inherited in plants?
cards.b: Yes, through asexual reproduction, e.g. a mutated branch propagated by cuttings (origin of navel oranges).

cards.f: Sickle cell allele in Africa: what does it show?
cards.b: A helpful germ-line mutation: heterozygous carriers are protected against malaria, so they survive and pass on the allele, keeping its frequency high.

cards.f: What proportion of the human genome is coding?
cards.b: Only about 1–2% (exons) of over 3 billion base pairs and ~20,000 genes; about 98% is non-coding.

cards.f: Significance of mutations in coding DNA?
cards.b: Directly alter the amino acid sequence and protein (sickle cell, CF), so more likely harmful; may be silent due to redundancy; mutations in repair and growth-control genes lead to cancer.

Satellite DNA (tandem repeats, STRs), Telomeres, Introns, Non-coding RNA genes (tRNA, rRNA, microRNA), Gene regulatory sequences (promoters, enhancers, silencers, terminators). Also centromeres and transposons.

cards.f: Effect of mutations in promoters and enhancers?
cards.b: Promoter: gene not transcribed, or at the wrong time or place. Enhancer/silencer: over- or under-expression. E.g. a TBX5 enhancer mutation causes congenital heart defects.

cards.f: Effect of mutations in introns and telomeres?
cards.b: Introns: usually no effect, but splice-site mutations cause incorrect splicing and abnormal proteins. Telomeres: shortening causes chromosome instability, ageing and cancer.

cards.f: Overall significance of coding vs non-coding mutations?
cards.b: Coding: directly alter proteins, single-gene disorders. Non-coding: mostly neutral (most SNPs), but regulatory mutations change gene expression, causing congenital abnormalities and disease predisposition; also a source of variation.

cards.f: Sources of genetic variation in sexual reproduction?
cards.b: Mutation (only source of NEW alleles), crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I), random segregation, random fertilisation.

cards.f: How does independent assortment cause variation?
cards.b: Random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I gives random mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes: 2^23 ≈ 8.4 million combinations per human gamete.
Random fusion of two haploid gametes from different parents restores 2n, combining two genomes; a couple could produce over 64 trillion genetically unique children.

cards.f: Define gene pool and allele frequency.
cards.b: Gene pool: all the genes and alleles in a reproducing population. Allele frequency: how often an allele occurs in the population.

cards.f: Five factors that change allele frequency (teacher)?
cards.b: 1. Selective pressure (natural selection) 2. Sexual selection (non-random mating) 3. Mutation 4. Genetic drift 5. Gene flow.

cards.f: Effect of mutation on the gene pool?
cards.b: Introduces new alleles (the ultimate source of variation), usually slowly; new alleles are then acted on by selection, drift or gene flow. Only germline mutations are passed on.

cards.f: Define gene flow and its effect.
cards.b: Migration of individuals or gametes (e.g. pollen) between populations. Adds or removes alleles, makes populations more similar and counteracts divergence. E.g. marine iguanas swimming between Galapagos islands.

cards.f: Define genetic drift and its effect.
cards.b: Random changes in allele frequency due to chance, not fitness. Reduces variation (alleles lost or fixed); biggest effect in small populations; can lead to divergence.

cards.f: What's the trap with genetic drift?
cards.b: Drift is change due to CHANCE, not natural selection. It makes populations different, not necessarily better adapted.
A sudden drastic reduction in population size from a chance event leaves survivors with unrepresentative allele frequencies. E.g. a bushfire leaves only brown-furred possums; cheetahs.
A small, non-representative group starts a new population, so it has reduced variation and different allele frequencies by chance. E.g. a few beetles blown to an island are mostly AA.

cards.f: Cheetah case study: what happened and what are the effects?
cards.b: Bottleneck about 10,000–20,000 years ago (end of the last ice age), possibly to one family group. Now under 20,000 in the wild with very low diversity: sperm abnormalities, low fertility, high cub mortality, disease sensitivity.

cards.f: Define horizontal gene transfer + three methods.
cards.b: Transfer of genes between organisms that are not parent and offspring (common in prokaryotes). Transformation (uptake of free DNA), transduction (phage carries DNA), conjugation (plasmid passed through a pilus).
It spreads antibiotic-resistance genes (often on plasmids) rapidly between bacteria, even across species, much faster than mutation and vertical inheritance alone.

cards.f: How does polyploidy cause instant speciation?
cards.b: A 4n plant crossed with the 2n parent gives sterile 3n offspring, so the polyploid is reproductively isolated at once: a new species in one generation (common in plants).
A geographic barrier divides a population; different selection pressures, mutations and drift with no gene flow make them diverge until they can no longer interbreed.
The manipulation of living organisms, or their components (cells, enzymes, genes), to produce useful products or processes for humans in medicine, agriculture, industry and the environment.
GMO: genome changed by genetic engineering. Transgenic: a GMO containing a gene from a different species. All transgenics are GMOs, but not all GMOs are transgenic (e.g. CRISPR knockout).
Ancient (>10,000 years ago–~1800): whole organisms, trial and error. Classical (~1800–mid 1900s): microbes and inheritance understood. Modern (1953/1970s–now): direct DNA manipulation.
Fermentation (bread, beer, wine, yoghurt, cheese), selective breeding and domestication (Fertile Crescent, ~10,000 years), Gunditjmara eel aquaculture at Budj Bim (>6,000 years), medicinal plants.

Pasteur (fermentation is biological; pasteurisation), Mendel (laws of inheritance), Buchner (1897, cell-free enzymes ferment sugar), Fleming (1928, penicillin; mass-produced by Florey and Chain), hybridisation.
Recombinant DNA (insulin), PCR, sequencing, DNA profiling, cloning, CRISPR, transgenic crops (Bt cotton), mRNA vaccines, spray-on skin, bioremediation.
Fiona Wood and Marie Stoner (Perth). A patient's healthy skin cells are cultured and sprayed on burns: a cultured epithelial autograft. No rejection; less scarring. Used after the 2002 Bali bombings.

cards.f: Embryonic vs adult vs induced pluripotent stem cells?
cards.b: Embryonic: pluripotent, from the blastocyst inner cell mass (embryo destroyed). Adult: multipotent (bone marrow). iPSCs: adult cells reprogrammed to pluripotency (Yamanaka, 2006), avoiding embryo use.
Personalised medicine/pharmacogenomics, synthetic biology, gene therapy, nanomedicine, 3D bioprinting of organs, AI (AlphaFold), biomanufacturing, de-extinction and conservation, gene drives.
Somatic: body cells only, not inherited (CF, SCID). Germline: gametes or embryos, inherited; banned in most countries including Australia.

cards.f: Social and ethical issues of biotechnology?
cards.b: Privacy, insurance/employment discrimination, GM food safety, 'playing God', designer babies, patents and company monopolies, animal welfare, bioterrorism, equity of access, biopiracy, labelling.
1. Benefit and non-harm 2. Individual rights and autonomy (informed consent) 3. Privacy and societal perception 4. Equity and justice.
Office of the Gene Technology Regulator (OGTR) regulates GMOs and release; Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) assesses GM food safety and labelling.

cards.f: Bt cotton: social and ethical positives and negatives?
cards.b: Positive: less spraying, better worker and community health, higher income, up to 85% less insecticide. Negative: expensive seed, Indian farmer debt, pest resistance, non-target concerns (Monarch debate), corporate seed ownership.

cards.f: Spider silk goats: what and why?
cards.b: Spider silk gene with a milk-protein promoter inserted into goats, so silk protein is made in milk (spiders can't be farmed). Uses: sutures, ligaments, body armour. Issues: welfare, animals as factories.

cards.f: Golden rice: what problem does it address?
cards.b: Vitamin A deficiency where rice is the staple: night blindness, permanent blindness (250,000–500,000 children a year), weakened immunity and death.

cards.f: Golden rice: genes inserted and method?
cards.b: psy (phytoene synthase) from daffodil (golden rice 2: maize) + crtI from the bacterium Pantoea (Erwinia) uredovora, inserted by Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Endosperm makes beta-carotene. NOT CRISPR, not carrot genes.

Approved by FSANZ (2017), Health Canada and US FDA (2018); Philippines first to approve planting (2021). Free seed for poor farmers. Opposed by Greenpeace; trials vandalised (2013); Philippine court halted planting (2024).

Benefits: reduces VAD blindness and death; free, saveable seed; no diet change. Limitations: 20+ years of delay, beta-carotene degrades in storage, doesn't fix poverty, cross-pollination and diversity concerns.

Chinook salmon growth hormone gene joined to an ocean pout antifreeze promoter (active all year) and microinjected into Atlantic salmon eggs. Reaches market size in 16–18 months instead of ~3 years, using ~25% less feed.

cards.f: AquAdvantage salmon: approval, safeguards and issues?
cards.b: First GM animal approved as food (US FDA, Nov 2015; Canada 2016). Safeguards: sterile triploid females in land-based tanks. Issues: escape risk, 'Frankenfish' labelling fight, wild fishery harm; AquaBounty closed farms in 2024.
About 22% higher yields, ~8% less pesticide, ~48 million acres saved from clearing (one year), lower CO2 emissions. Over 99% of Australian cotton is GM.

cards.f: Benefits for society of research using genetic technologies?
cards.b: Medicine (insulin, vaccines, screening, Human Genome Project), agriculture (yield, nutrition), environment (less chemical use, conservation), industry (enzymes, biofuels), forensics. Depends on equitable access and regulation.
Genetic diversity (alleles within a species), species diversity (number and abundance of species), ecosystem diversity (variety of ecosystems).

Monocultures (1970 corn blight), elite parents in AI and cloning, loss of heritage varieties, gene flow to wild relatives (superweeds), harm to non-target species, escaped transgenic animals, gene drives, resistance.

cards.f: Ways genetic techniques increase or preserve biodiversity?
cards.b: Transgenes add new alleles, conservation cloning and IVF (black-footed ferret Elizabeth Ann, 2020; northern white rhino), seed banks (Svalbard), less land cleared, less pesticide, removing invasive species.

cards.f: Genetic techniques and biodiversity: short-term vs long-term?
cards.b: Short term: transgenes add new alleles to a species. Long term: monocultures and elite parents reduce allele variety, so populations are less able to adapt to disease and change.

cards.f: Southern white rhino: what does it show?
cards.b: Conservation through captive breeding and AI: about 50 left in the early 1900s, over 20,400 at the peak; poaching has since cut numbers to ~16,000–17,000. Kept in separate populations to spread risk.

cards.f: Eugenics: why is it an ethical concern?
cards.b: The idea of 'improving' humans by controlling breeding justified forced sterilisations and Nazi atrocities; modern screening raises fears of a 'new eugenics' and designer babies.
An international agreement ensuring fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources, e.g. indigenous communities benefit when their plants are used for drugs (counters biopiracy).
Reproductive technology manipulates reproduction (AI, AP, IVF, cloning) without directly altering the DNA sequence. Genetic technology alters or uses the genetic material directly.
Using prostaglandins, progestins (CIDR) or GnRH so many females ovulate at once before AI or embryo transfer; easier management.

1. Choose a male with desirable traits 2. Collect semen 3. Check, dilute with extender, freeze in straws (−196 °C) 4. Synchronise females or detect heat 5. Thaw and place in cervix/uterus 6. Confirm pregnancy.
A Holstein bull (not a cow) who sired over 200,000 daughters by AI, showing AI's reach and its narrowing of the gene pool. Cloned in 2000 (Starbuck II).

1. Choose parent plants 2. Emasculate the female parent (remove stamens) 3. Bag the flower 4. Collect pollen from the male parent 5. Brush onto the stigma 6. Re-bag, label, collect seeds 7. Grow and select.

cards.f: 1970 Southern corn leaf blight: what does it show?
cards.b: About 85% of US corn used the genetically uniform Tcms line; the fungus destroyed ~15% of the crop (~US$1 billion). Shows how AP and uniformity reduce biodiversity and increase vulnerability.

cards.f: Compare artificial insemination and artificial pollination.
cards.b: Similar: human-controlled transfer of male gametes, selective breeding, sexual reproduction (varied offspring), no direct DNA change, reduce diversity. Different: animals vs plants; semen into tract vs pollen onto stigma; semen frozen for decades vs pollen stored briefly.

1. FSH injections (superovulation) 2. Collect eggs by ultrasound-guided needle 3. Prepare sperm 4. Fertilise in a dish (or ICSI) 5. Culture 3–5 days, optional PGD 6. Transfer embryo 7. Pregnancy test ~2 weeks.

cards.f: What's the trap with IVF and ICSI?
cards.b: Injecting a single sperm into an egg with a needle is ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), a specific type of assisted fertilisation, not standard IVF.
Louise Brown, 25 July 1978, England (Steptoe and Edwards). Australia's first: Candice Reed, 1980, Melbourne.

cards.f: Whole organism vs therapeutic vs gene cloning?
cards.b: Whole organism: a clone animal (Dolly) via SCNT or embryo splitting. Therapeutic: patient-matched embryonic stem cells. Gene cloning: many copies of a gene and its protein (insulin) via plasmids.

1. Udder cell from Finn Dorset ewe 2. Starve cell to G0 3. Enucleate a Scottish Blackface egg 4. Fuse with electric pulse (also activates division) 5. Culture embryo ~6 days 6. Implant into Blackface surrogate 7. White-faced clone born.

Roslin Institute (Wilmut, Campbell). Born 5 July 1996, announced Feb 1997. First mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. 277 fused eggs → 29 embryos → 1 lamb. Arthritis and lung disease; euthanased Feb 2003 at ~6.5 years.

cards.f: Why is a clone not 100% identical?
cards.b: Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg donor, epigenetic differences exist, and the environment affects the phenotype.
An early IVF embryo (e.g. 8-cell) is split into groups, each implanted into surrogates; offspring are clones of each other, not of the parents. Tetra the rhesus macaque (1999).

cards.f: Assess the effectiveness of whole organism cloning.
cards.b: Effective: exact copies of elite genotypes, faster than breeding, conservation, easy in plants. Limited: ~1–5% success, health problems, no new variation, ethical issues. Judgement: effective in plants and limited high-value animal uses.

cards.f: Steps of gene cloning using a plasmid?
cards.b: 1. Cut gene out with restriction enzyme (or make cDNA) 2. Cut plasmid with same enzyme 3. Mix; sticky ends pair; ligase seals 4. Transform bacteria (heat shock/CaCl2) 5. Select on antibiotic agar 6. Culture 7. Extract protein.

cards.f: Assess the effectiveness of gene cloning.
cards.b: Highly effective, cheap and reliable: bacteria copy and express the gene each division, producing large amounts of protein (insulin). Transformation is inefficient (~1 in 10,000 cells), but selection solves this.

cards.f: Why use cDNA when cloning a human gene in bacteria?
cards.b: cDNA is made from mRNA by reverse transcriptase, so it has no introns; bacteria cannot remove introns.
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific (usually palindromic) recognition sequence by breaking phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone. E.g. EcoRI cuts G^AATTC.

cards.f: What's the trap with restriction enzymes?
cards.b: They break phosphodiester bonds in the backbone, not hydrogen bonds. DNA ligase re-forms the same phosphodiester bonds (ligation is the reverse).
Sticky ends: short single-stranded overhangs from a staggered cut that base-pair with complementary ends. Blunt ends: straight cut, no overhang (e.g. SmaI).

cards.f: Two steps to join DNA fragments?
cards.b: 1. Annealing: complementary sticky ends form hydrogen bonds (temporary). 2. DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds, sealing both backbones permanently.

cards.f: How many fragments from n restriction cuts?
cards.b: Linear DNA: n cuts give n + 1 fragments. Circular plasmid: n cuts give n fragments.
Plasmid: small circular DNA in bacteria that replicates independently; used as a vector. Marker gene: e.g. antibiotic resistance or GFP, showing which cells took up the vector.

cards.f: General steps to make a transgenic organism?
cards.b: 1. Isolate gene 2. Insert into vector with promoter and marker 3. Introduce into host cells 4. Select transformed cells 5. Grow into whole organisms 6. Test expression and inheritance; safety trials.

cards.f: Why can a human gene work in bacteria?
cards.b: The genetic code is universal, so the transferred gene is transcribed and translated into the same protein.
Kary Mullis, 1983 (Nobel 1993). Template DNA, two primers, free nucleotides (dNTPs), Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus), buffer with Mg2+, in a thermocycler.

cards.f: Three steps of PCR with temperatures?
cards.b: 1. Denaturation ~95 °C: hydrogen bonds break, strands separate. 2. Annealing ~55 °C: primers bind. 3. Extension ~72 °C: Taq adds nucleotides to the 3' end of primers.

cards.f: How many copies after 30 PCR cycles?
cards.b: Each cycle doubles the DNA: 2^30 ≈ 1 billion copies, in a few hours.

cards.f: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
cards.b: It comes from a hot-spring bacterium, so it is not denatured at ~95 °C; new enzyme need not be added each cycle.

Uses: STR DNA profiling, paternity, COVID-19 RT-PCR, genetic disorder testing, ancient DNA, eDNA. Limitations: need known end sequences for primers, contamination amplified, errors copied, short sequences, no protein made.

cards.f: How does gel electrophoresis separate DNA?
cards.b: DNA is negatively charged (phosphates), so it moves to the positive electrode; smaller fragments travel further. A DNA ladder gives size; stain (e.g. ethidium bromide under UV) shows bands.
A bacterial immune system against viruses adapted for gene editing by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier (2012; Nobel Chemistry 2020).

1. Design guide RNA (~20 nt match) 2. Deliver gRNA + Cas9 3. gRNA guides Cas9 to target next to a PAM (e.g. NGG) 4. Cas9 makes a double-strand break 5. Repair: NHEJ (knockout) or HDR with template (insert/correct).
Advantages: precise, cheap, fast, multiple genes, no foreign DNA needed. Risks: off-target cuts, mosaicism, delivery difficulty, germline ethics (He Jiankui CCR5 twins, 2018, jailed), gene drives.
Non-browning apples and mushrooms; disease-resistant crops; sickle cell and beta-thalassaemia therapy (Casgevy, 2023); gene drives against invasive species; gene function research.

Microinjection (animal eggs), biolistics/gene gun (plant cells), electroporation (pores by electric pulse), viral vectors (gene therapy), Agrobacterium Ti plasmid (dicot plants), heat shock/CaCl2 (bacteria), liposomes.
CSIRO with Monsanto; Ingard released 1996, Bollgard II (two Bt genes) 2004. cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis inserted via Agrobacterium; cells grown by tissue culture.

cards.f: How does the Bt toxin kill only caterpillars?
cards.b: The Cry protoxin is activated in the alkaline caterpillar gut and binds specific gut receptors, making pores so the gut ruptures and feeding stops. Mammals and most insects lack the receptors and have acidic stomachs.
Refuge crops (non-Bt cotton or pigeon pea) so susceptible insects mate with resistant ones, integrated pest management, crop rotation, and stacking two or more toxin genes (Bollgard II, 3).

cards.f: Recombinant human insulin: steps and benefits?
cards.b: Human insulin gene (or cDNA/synthetic A and B chain genes) inserted into plasmids → E. coli → grown in fermenters → insulin purified. Humulin approved 1982. Benefits: identical to human, fewer allergies, unlimited, no animals killed.
Human antithrombin III gene with a goat beta-casein (milk) promoter microinjected into embryos; protein purified from milk. Approved Europe 2006, USA 2009. One goat ≈ 90,000 blood donations a year.
Roundup Ready crops (glyphosate tolerance), Flavr Savr tomato (1994), recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (yeast), OncoMouse (1988), GloFish, blue roses (pansy genes), high-cysteine alfalfa for wool.

cards.f: Antifreeze tomatoes and strawberries: checked fact?
cards.b: The antifreeze gene came from the winter flounder fish (not salmon). Experimental frost resistance; never commercialised.
1. Identify faulty gene (CFTR, ADA) 2. Make functional copy 3. Insert into vector (modified virus or liposome) 4. Deliver in vivo or ex vivo 5. Gene expressed, normal protein made.
Immune reaction to vector (Jesse Gelsinger died, 1999), insertion in the wrong place causing cancer (leukaemia in SCID trials), high cost, temporary effects.
Oil-eating bacteria (first patented GMO, Chakrabarty, 1980), plastic-degrading microbes, algae biofuel, enzymes in detergents, bioplastics, bioleaching in mining.

cards.f: Evaluate benefits of genetic technologies (agriculture, medicine, industry).
cards.b: Agriculture: ~22% yield, less pesticide (Bt cotton, golden rice). Medicine: safe human proteins, vaccines, diagnosis (insulin, PCR). Industry: cleaner processes, biofuels. Limits: resistance, cost, biodiversity loss, ethics.

cards.f: How do social, economic and cultural contexts influence biotechnology?
cards.b: Social (public opinion, NGOs) affects acceptance; economic (cost, patents, funding) affects development and access; cultural (religion, food traditions, indigenous values) affects acceptance and regulation.

cards.f: Golden rice: social, economic and cultural contexts?
cards.b: Social: VAD need vs Greenpeace opposition. Economic: patents donated; foundation-funded (Rockefeller, Gates). Cultural: rice a staple; some object to yellow or GM rice.
Pigs whose cells carry human surface proteins so their organs are less likely to trigger rejection, addressing organ shortages; raises animal welfare issues.

cards.f: Exam structure: 'explain' how a mutagen affects a population (4 marks)?
cards.b: 1. Define the mutagen. 2. Step through the biology: DNA altered → protein synthesis changed → abnormalities. 3. Link to the scenario ('hence'): more exposure, more mutations.

cards.f: Exam structure: contrast frameshift vs substitution on a given sequence?
cards.b: Write the sequence in triplets; under a Frameshift heading define and apply (all later codons change); under Substitution define and apply (one codon); use 'in contrast' and quote the sequence.

cards.f: Exam structure: evaluate effects of genetic techniques on biodiversity?
cards.b: Opening judgement; decreases (monocultures, 1970 corn blight, elite parents, gene flow, superweeds) vs increases (new alleles, conservation, less land cleared); short vs long term; final judgement.
A disease-causing agent, cellular or non-cellular, that infects a host and disrupts its normal function.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted from one host to another, directly or indirectly.
An organism (often an insect) that carries a pathogen from one host to another without itself getting the disease, e.g. the Anopheles mosquito for malaria.
A population or environment where a pathogen normally lives and multiplies, e.g. flying foxes for Hendra virus and fruit bats for Ebola. A reservoir is not a vector.
A misfolded protein (non-cellular, no nucleic acid) that converts normal proteins into the misfolded form, causing brain damage. Examples: BSE (mad cow disease), vCJD, kuru.
A non-cellular pathogen of DNA or RNA in a protein capsid (sometimes with an envelope) that can only replicate inside host cells. Examples: influenza, HIV, COVID-19, dengue.
Prokaryotic cells (no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, cell wall of peptidoglycan) that reproduce by binary fission; some produce toxins. Examples: TB, cholera, Salmonella, pinkeye.
Single-celled eukaryotes, often with complex life cycles and vectors. Examples: Plasmodium (malaria), Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease), T. brucei (African sleeping sickness).
Eukaryotes that grow as hyphae or yeasts and spread by spores. Examples: tinea (athlete's foot), thrush, myrtle rust, wheat stem rust, Panama disease.
Multicellular parasites visible to the naked eye, living on (ecto-) or in (endo-) the host. Examples: tapeworms (hydatids), ticks, lice, fleas.

cards.f: What type of organism is Phytophthora?
cards.b: An oomycete (water mould), not a true fungus. It causes root rot (dieback) in plants.

cards.f: What is the chain of infection?
cards.b: Pathogen, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Breaking any link stops spread.

cards.f: List the main modes of disease transmission.
cards.b: Direct contact, indirect contact (fomites), droplet/airborne, contaminated food and water, body fluids (blood-borne, sexual), and vectors.

cards.f: What share of infectious diseases are vector-borne?
cards.b: More than 17% of all infectious diseases.

cards.f: Where did the 2007 equine influenza outbreak in Australia start?
cards.b: It escaped from Eastern Creek quarantine station and spread at Centennial Park, Sydney.

cards.f: How was the 2007 equine influenza outbreak controlled?
cards.b: A national standstill on horse movement, response coordinated from Orange and Menangle, zoning, and targeted (not mass) vaccination. Cases peaked at about 1,000 a week; controlled by December 2007 and Australia declared free in early 2008.

cards.f: Why is mass vaccination not used against equine influenza?
cards.b: The virus mutates, vaccinated horses can still spread it, and vaccination would mask infection and delay detection.

cards.f: Which receptor does SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) use to enter cells?
cards.b: The ACE2 receptor.

cards.f: What are the types of influenza virus?
cards.b: Types A, B and C. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A, named after its haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface proteins.

Drift: small, gradual mutations in surface antigens, causing seasonal flu and yearly vaccine updates. Shift: sudden major change when two strains swap genes (e.g. in pigs), producing a new subtype that can cause a pandemic.

cards.f: How many people did the 1918 influenza pandemic infect?
cards.b: About one-third of the world's population, around 500 million people.

cards.f: How does tuberculosis (TB) survive the immune system?
cards.b: Its waxy cell wall resists digestion inside macrophages, and the body walls it off in granulomas where it can stay dormant.

cards.f: How does Plasmodium (malaria) evade the immune system?
cards.b: Antigenic variation (changing surface proteins) and hypnozoites, dormant liver stages that cause relapse.

cards.f: What did John Snow show in 1854?
cards.b: He mapped cholera cases in London and traced them to the Broad Street water pump, showing cholera was waterborne. Removing the pump handle stopped cases; this founded epidemiology.

Broth in a swan-neck flask stayed sterile because microbes were trapped in the bent neck; when the neck was broken, the broth went cloudy. This disproved spontaneous generation and supported germ theory.
Heating liquids (e.g. milk) to a temperature that kills most pathogens without spoiling them, developed by Pasteur.
Chicken cholera (1879), anthrax (1881) and rabies (1885). (Smallpox was Jenner; BCG was Calmette and Guérin.)

cards.f: Which pathogens did Koch identify, and when?
cards.b: Anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883).

1. The microbe is found in all diseased hosts, not healthy ones. 2. It is isolated and grown in pure culture. 3. It causes the same disease when given to a healthy host. 4. It is re-isolated and identical to the original.
Viruses and prions cannot be grown in pure culture; some people are asymptomatic carriers; some pathogens infect only humans (unethical to test); some diseases have several causes.

cards.f: What did Barry Marshall do in 1984?
cards.b: He drank a culture of Helicobacter pylori and developed gastritis, proving the bacterium causes stomach ulcers. Marshall and Warren won the Nobel Prize in 2005.

cards.f: What caused the Irish potato famine and why was it so severe?
cards.b: Phytophthora infestans (potato blight). Ireland relied on one variety (Lumper) as a monoculture with no resistance; about 1 million people died.

A fungal disease of bananas caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc) Tropical Race 4. It blocks the xylem, wilting the plant; there is no chemical cure, so quarantine and resistant varieties are used.
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease), a prion disease spread through feed containing infected meat and bone meal. Incubation 2-8 years; the UK epidemic peaked in 1993.

cards.f: How is BSE linked to humans, and how does Australia prevent it?
cards.b: Eating infected beef can cause variant CJD (about 230 cases worldwide). Australia bans feeding ruminant material to ruminants.

cards.f: Why is vaccination not a valid control for prawn diseases?
cards.b: Prawns (invertebrates) have no adaptive immune system, so they cannot form memory cells.

cards.f: How do pathogens adapt to infect hosts?
cards.b: Adhesion (attaching via pili or proteins), invasins (entering cells), toxins, and evading immunity (capsules, antigenic variation, hiding inside cells).

cards.f: Outline how HIV infects a T helper cell.
cards.b: gp120 binds CD4 and the CCR5 co-receptor; the envelope fuses and RNA enters; reverse transcriptase makes DNA; integrase inserts it into host DNA; the cell makes viral proteins; protease cuts them; new virions assemble and bud out.

cards.f: Why do only female mosquitoes transmit disease?
cards.b: Only females bite, because they need a blood meal to produce eggs.

cards.f: Which mosquito-borne diseases now have vaccines?
cards.b: Yellow fever, dengue (Qdenga) and malaria (RTS,S and R21).

cards.f: Which painkillers should be avoided with dengue fever, and why?
cards.b: Ibuprofen and aspirin (NSAIDs), because they increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is used instead.

Passive: present before infection (waxy cuticle, bark, cell walls, stomata, antimicrobial chemicals). Active: triggered by infection (oxidative burst, callose, phytoalexins, hypersensitive response, SAR).
Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) detect pathogen molecules; in gene-for-gene resistance, a plant R gene product matches a pathogen Avr gene product and triggers defence.

cards.f: What is the oxidative burst in plants?
cards.b: Rapid production of reactive oxygen species such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) that kill pathogens and strengthen cell walls.

cards.f: What role does callose play in plant defence?
cards.b: It is deposited in cell walls and blocks plasmodesmata, stopping the pathogen (especially viruses) moving between cells.
Antimicrobial chemicals made by plants after infection that kill or slow pathogens.

cards.f: What is the hypersensitive response in plants?
cards.b: Rapid, programmed death of cells around the infection site, depriving the pathogen of living tissue and stopping its spread.
A whole-plant, long-lasting resistance after a local infection, signalled by salicylic acid.
A fungal disease (Austropuccinia psidii) detected in Australia in 2010. Purple spots then yellow pustules on new growth; affects over 380 species in the Myrtaceae family.

cards.f: What causes pinkeye in cattle and how is it treated?
cards.b: The bacterium Moraxella bovis, spread by flies. Treated with antibiotics such as Orbenin and oxytetracycline, plus eye patches and fly control.
Signalling proteins released by cells (e.g. interleukins, interferons, chemokines) that communicate between immune cells and coordinate the response.
Cytokines released by virus-infected cells that make neighbouring cells switch on interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) to resist viral replication.

cards.f: Which cells release most inflammatory chemicals?
cards.b: Mast cells and basophils release heparin, histamine and serotonin. Prostaglandins are made by nearly all cells.
Self: molecules (MHC markers) on the body's own cells, which the immune system tolerates. Non-self: foreign antigens, which trigger a response.
A molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that the immune system recognises as foreign and that triggers an immune response.
Innate: non-specific, rapid, present from birth, no memory (1st and 2nd lines). Adaptive: specific to an antigen, slower at first, produces memory (3rd line: B and T cells).

cards.f: List first-line physical barriers in humans.
cards.b: Intact skin (keratin, shedding), mucous membranes and mucus, cilia that sweep mucus out, and flushing by tears, urine, saliva, vomiting and diarrhoea.

cards.f: List first-line chemical barriers in humans.
cards.b: Lysozyme in tears, saliva and sweat; stomach HCl; acidic skin and vagina; and normal microflora that outcompete pathogens.
No. Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and cancer cells lacking MHC I.
No. Mast cells release histamine and other inflammatory chemicals; they do not engulf pathogens.

1. Chemotaxis to the pathogen. 2. Adherence. 3. Engulfing by pseudopodia. 4. Phagosome forms. 5. Lysosome fuses (phagolysosome). 6. Enzymes digest the pathogen. 7. Waste is expelled; antigens may be presented on MHC II.

cards.f: What are the five cardinal signs of inflammation?
cards.b: Redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function.

Damaged cells and mast cells release histamine and prostaglandins, causing vasodilation (redness, heat) and increased capillary permeability, so fluid, proteins and white blood cells enter the tissue (swelling, pain).

cards.f: How does fever help fight infection?
cards.b: IL-1 acts on the hypothalamus, which releases prostaglandins and raises the body's set point. Higher temperature slows pathogen growth and speeds immune cell activity.
Plasma proteins that lyse pathogens by making pores, opsonise them for phagocytosis, and boost inflammation.

cards.f: What is the role of the lymphatic system in immunity?
cards.b: About 90% of tissue fluid returns to capillaries and 10% becomes lymph. Lymph carries pathogens and APCs to lymph nodes, where B and T cells are activated.

MHC I: on all nucleated cells, shows internal (e.g. viral) antigens to cytotoxic T cells. MHC II: only on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells), shows antigens to helper T cells.
Only the lymphocyte whose receptor matches the antigen is selected, activated and divides by mitosis into many identical clones (effector and memory cells).
A Y-shaped protein of 4 polypeptide chains (2 heavy, 2 light) with 2 identical antigen-binding sites at the variable region tips.

cards.f: How do antibodies work? (they don't kill directly)
cards.b: They neutralise toxins and viruses, agglutinate (clump) pathogens, precipitate soluble antigens, opsonise for phagocytosis, and activate complement.

cards.f: How do cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells?
cards.b: They bind cells showing the antigen on MHC I and release perforin (makes pores) and granzymes (enzymes), or use Fas ligand, triggering apoptosis.

cards.f: List the T cell types and roles.
cards.b: Helper (CD4+): activate B and cytotoxic T cells with cytokines. Cytotoxic (CD8+): kill infected cells. Suppressor/regulatory: switch the response off. Memory: long-term immunity.

cards.f: List the B cell types and roles.
cards.b: Plasma cells secrete specific antibodies. Memory B cells persist for years and give a fast secondary response.

cards.f: Where do B and T cells mature?
cards.b: B cells in the bone marrow; T cells in the thymus.

cards.f: Immune sequence step 1-2: what happens at the first line?
cards.b: The pathogen meets barriers (skin, mucus, cilia, secretions, microflora). If a barrier is breached, e.g. a cut, it enters, multiplies and is detected as foreign by its non-self antigens (PAMPs).

cards.f: Immune sequence step 3: which cells respond first inside the body?
cards.b: Resident macrophages phagocytose the pathogen and release cytokines and chemokines to call other immune cells.

cards.f: Immune sequence step 4: what happens in inflammation?
cards.b: Mast cells and injured cells release histamine; vasodilation and increased capillary permeability let fluid, complement, clotting factors and white blood cells leave the blood into the tissue.

cards.f: Immune sequence step 5: what do neutrophils do?
cards.b: Arrive in large numbers (attracted by chemokines), phagocytose pathogens and release toxic chemicals; dead neutrophils form pus.

cards.f: Immune sequence step 6: which other innate defences act?
cards.b: Complement lyses and opsonises; interferons protect neighbouring cells; NK cells kill infected cells lacking MHC I; fever raises the set point via IL-1.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 7-8: how is the adaptive response triggered?
cards.b: Dendritic cells (and macrophages) engulf the pathogen, display its antigen on MHC II as APCs, and travel through lymph to the nearest lymph node, where naive B and T cells wait.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 9-10: what happens to helper T cells?
cards.b: The APC binds the helper T cell (CD4+) with the matching receptor; it is activated and clones. Helper T cells release interleukins (e.g. IL-2) that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells and boost macrophages.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 11-12: how is a B cell activated?
cards.b: A B cell binds the matching antigen and presents it on MHC II; the matching helper T cell binds and releases interleukins. The B cell clones and differentiates into plasma cells and memory B cells.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 13-14: what happens in the humoral branch?
cards.b: Plasma cells secrete millions of specific antibodies, which bind antigens to neutralise, agglutinate, precipitate, opsonise and activate complement, so macrophages and neutrophils destroy the pathogens.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 15-16: what happens in the cell-mediated branch?
cards.b: Matching cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) are activated and clone, then kill body cells displaying the antigen on MHC I using perforins, granzymes or Fas ligand (apoptosis).

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 17-19: how does the response end?
cards.b: The pathogen is cleared; suppressor T cells switch off the response; most effector cells die by apoptosis; memory B and T cells remain for years.

cards.f: Immune sequence steps 20-21: what happens on re-exposure?
cards.b: Memory B cells quickly become plasma cells and memory T cells divide into effector T cells. The response is faster, stronger and longer, usually destroying the pathogen before symptoms appear.

cards.f: Give the one-line pocket version of the immune response.
cards.b: Barriers; phagocytes, inflammation, fever, complement, interferon, NK cells; APC presents on MHC II at lymph node; helper T activated; B cells to plasma cells and antibodies, or cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; suppressor T cells switch off; memory cells remain.

cards.f: Humoral vs cell-mediated response: which pathogens does each target?
cards.b: Humoral (B cells, antibodies) targets extracellular pathogens and toxins in body fluids. Cell-mediated (cytotoxic T cells) targets intracellular pathogens by killing infected cells.
Primary: first exposure, lag of 7-14 days, small short antibody peak. Secondary: memory cells respond in 1-3 days with a much larger, longer-lasting antibody peak.

cards.f: Natural active vs artificial active immunity?
cards.b: Natural active: making your own antibodies and memory after infection. Artificial active: after vaccination. Both are long-lasting.

cards.f: Natural passive vs artificial passive immunity?
cards.b: Natural passive: antibodies from mother via placenta or breast milk. Artificial passive: injected antibodies (e.g. antivenom). Immediate but short-lived, no memory.

cards.f: What did the mouse skin-graft experiment show?
cards.b: A second graft from the same donor was rejected faster than the first, showing immunological memory (a secondary response) by T cells.

cards.f: What factors affect spread of disease at local, regional and global levels?
cards.b: Local: hygiene, sanitation, housing density. Regional: climate, vectors, healthcare access. Global: travel, trade, migration and climate change.

cards.f: Outline the malaria life cycle in humans.
