cards.b: An infected female Anopheles injects sporozoites; they travel to the liver and multiply, then infect red blood cells, which burst in cycles (fever). Gametocytes are taken up by another mosquito. About half the world is at risk.
Prevention stops disease occurring (vaccination, hygiene). Control limits spread once present (quarantine, treatment, vector control).
Quarantine: separating people or goods that may have been exposed, until shown not infected. Isolation: separating people known to be infected.
In 1796-98 he showed that cowpox material protected against smallpox, the first vaccine.
Certified by the WHO commission in December 1979; formally declared by the World Health Assembly in May 1980 (standard answer: 1980).

Lipid-coated mRNA enters cells, which make the pathogen's antigen (e.g. spike protein). The immune system responds and forms memory cells. The mRNA does not enter the nucleus or alter DNA and breaks down quickly.

cards.f: What is herd immunity and its threshold?
cards.b: When enough people are immune, transmission chains break and unvaccinated people are protected. Threshold = 1 - 1/R0; measles needs about 95%.
Salk: inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), injected, 1955. Sabin: live-attenuated oral vaccine (OPV), 1961.

cards.f: What has the Global Polio Eradication Initiative achieved?
cards.b: Since 1988 (WHO, UNICEF, Rotary, CDC), cases have fallen by more than 99%; wild polio is endemic only in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

cards.f: What are the four main vaccine types?
cards.b: Live-attenuated (weakened pathogen), inactivated (killed pathogen), subunit/recombinant (pieces such as a protein) and toxoid (inactivated toxin).
They contain only harmless parts, or killed or weakened forms, which still carry antigens that trigger a primary response and memory cells.

cards.f: Why does influenza's high mutation rate matter?
cards.b: Antigenic drift changes surface antigens, so memory cells don't recognise them; the response is slower, people are infectious longer, and vaccines must be updated yearly.

cards.f: What happened to US measles cases after the 1963 vaccine?
cards.b: They fell from hundreds of thousands a year to negligible levels by about 1990, due to artificial active immunity and herd immunity (R0 about 12-18).

cards.f: What does RICE stand for in public health?
cards.b: Resolution, Information, Coordination, Education: the government approach to controlling infectious disease.
Diseases that must by law be reported when detected, so outbreaks are caught early. Examples: measles, cholera, botulism, meningococcal, pertussis, malaria.

cards.f: Outline DDT's history in disease control.
cards.b: Used in WWII against lice spreading typhus, then against Anopheles mosquitoes. Mosquitoes evolved resistance; banned in many countries (US 1972) for bioaccumulation and eggshell thinning. Müller discovered its action in 1939 (Nobel 1948).
Resistance (Colorado potato beetle resists more than 50 insecticides), harm to non-target species, environmental damage and human toxicity.

They carry a Bacillus thuringiensis gene for Cry protein. Pests eating the plant have alkaline guts with receptors; the protein ruptures the gut and kills them. Humans' acidic digestion breaks it down and we lack the receptors.

cards.f: How is resistance to Bt crops managed?
cards.b: Refuge planting of non-Bt crops so susceptible pests survive and keep resistance alleles rare, plus crop rotation, monitoring and IPM.

A CRISPR-Cas9 system built into a genome that raises inheritance of an altered gene above 50%, e.g. to spread malaria resistance or infertility through mosquitoes. Concerns: ecological effects and irreversibility.
Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria; bacteriostatic antibiotics stop them growing and reproducing so the immune system can clear them.
Antibiotics target structures unique to bacteria (peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosomes, folate synthesis), so they harm the pathogen but not host cells.
Broad-spectrum act on many bacteria (Gram-positive and negative), used when the cause is unknown but also kill normal flora. Narrow-spectrum act on one or a few types, e.g. penicillin.
Gram-positive keep the violet stain (thick peptidoglycan). Gram-negative stain pink/red and have an extra outer membrane making them more antibiotic-resistant.
It blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall, so water enters by osmosis and the bacterium bursts (osmotic lysis). Animal cells have no peptidoglycan.

cards.f: How do tetracyclines and erythromycin work?
cards.b: They bind bacterial 70S ribosomes: tetracycline (30S) blocks tRNA attachment; erythromycin (50S) blocks translocation, stopping protein synthesis.

cards.f: How do quinolones and sulfonamides work?
cards.b: Quinolones (ciprofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase, blocking DNA replication. Sulfonamides compete with PABA, blocking folate synthesis needed for nucleotides.

Random mutation gives a few resistant bacteria; antibiotics kill the rest (selection pressure); survivors reproduce by binary fission and share resistance genes on plasmids by conjugation; the population becomes resistant (superbug, e.g. MRSA).
Enzymes that destroy the drug (beta-lactamase), efflux pumps that pump it out, and changes that block it entering or alter its target.

cards.f: Human causes of and responses to antibiotic resistance?
cards.b: Causes: prescribing for viruses, not finishing courses, use in livestock. Responses: prescribe only when needed, finish courses, reserve last-resort drugs, new drugs, rapid diagnostics (Longitude Prize), phage therapy.

Strengths: highly effective, selective toxicity, cheap. Limitations: useless against viruses, rising resistance, kill normal flora, side effects, few new classes. Effective but declining, so stewardship is essential.
They inhibit a stage of the viral life cycle (entry, genome replication, protein synthesis, assembly or release), lowering viral load. They don't destroy viruses.

cards.f: Give examples of antivirals and their targets.
cards.b: Maraviroc blocks CCR5 entry (HIV); AZT inhibits reverse transcriptase (HIV); acyclovir inhibits herpes DNA polymerase; protease inhibitors (HIV); oseltamivir (Tamiflu) blocks neuraminidase, stopping influenza release.

cards.f: What does combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV target?
cards.b: Reverse transcriptase (AZT, tenofovir), integrase (dolutegravir), protease (protease inhibitors) and entry/fusion (maraviroc). It makes HIV a manageable chronic disease.

cards.f: Why are antivirals limited in effectiveness?
cards.b: Viruses use host machinery, so few safe targets exist; they mutate rapidly so resistance develops; development is expensive; they work best early; many strains (common cold: more than 200 viruses).

Vaccines: given before infection, stimulate antibodies and memory (artificial active immunity). Antivirals: given after infection, inhibit replication, no memory. Both reduce impact and spread of viral disease.

cards.f: Give environmental management methods to control epidemics.
cards.b: Safe water (boiling, chlorination), food hygiene and storage, sealed sewers and safe waste disposal, ventilation, and removing vector habitats (draining water, larvicides).

cards.f: Key facts on the 2014-16 West African Ebola epidemic?
cards.b: Mainly Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia; about 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths; death rate about 50%; incubation 2-21 days; fruit bats are the reservoir; spread person to person via bodily fluids.

PPE, handwashing, isolation, contact tracing with 21-day monitoring, safe burials, avoiding bushmeat, disinfection; rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine trialled near the end. The slow early response showed the need for rapid surveillance.

cards.f: Define incidence and give the formula.
cards.b: The number of new cases in a population at risk over a period. Incidence rate = new cases ÷ population at risk × 100 (or 100,000).
The proportion of a population that has the disease (new and existing cases) at a point or period. It rises with higher incidence or longer survival and falls with death or cure.

cards.f: How do mobility and immunisation rate affect disease incidence?
cards.b: Mobility spreads disease to new areas and non-immune people. High immunisation coverage gives herd immunity and lowers incidence; falling below threshold brings outbreaks back.

cards.f: Malaria vs dengue: cause and vector?
cards.b: Malaria: Plasmodium protozoa, female Anopheles mosquito biting dawn, dusk and night. Dengue: dengue virus (4 serotypes), female Aedes aegypti and albopictus biting by day in urban areas.
Malaria: antimalarials (ACTs, chloroquine, mefloquine). Dengue: supportive only (fluids, paracetamol, no NSAIDs); no specific antiviral.
About 249 million cases (2022, WHO) and about 600,000 deaths a year, mostly African children under 5. Endemic in more than 85 countries.
About 100-400 million infections a year (estimated 390 million, 96 million with symptoms), roughly 20,000-40,000 deaths. About 3.9 billion people in 128 countries are at risk.
India: cases down 36% and incidence down 45% (2000-2010). Five of 10 endemic SE Asian countries cut cases by more than 75% (2000-2011). Sri Lanka certified malaria-free in 2016.

cards.f: What factors affect the distribution of mosquito-borne disease?
cards.b: Environmental: temperature, rainfall, humidity, climate change. Social: poor healthcare funding, stored water and junk as breeding sites, unplanned urbanisation, globalisation and travel.

cards.f: When and where was quarantine first used?
cards.b: 1377 in Ragusa (now Dubrovnik, Croatia) against plague; ships were held for 30, then 40 days ('quaranta giorni').
Miasma theory, bloodletting, herbal remedies and quarantine largely failed: the Black Death killed about 30-60% of Europe. Quarantine was sound but rats and fleas weren't understood.

Variolation, Jenner's vaccination, Chadwick's sanitation reform (1834), Snow's epidemiology (1854), pasteurisation and Koch's postulates were very effective and form the scientific basis of modern control.

cards.f: Evaluate current strategies for predicting disease spread.
cards.b: WHO surveillance, event-based surveillance (GPHIN), web-based surveillance, modelling and genomic sequencing allow fast responses. Limits: depend on reporting and funding; Google Flu Trends overestimated flu and was discontinued.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge and practices for health, passed down over tens of thousands of years, including prevention, diagnosis and spiritual and emotional wellbeing. Raw materials for drugs are called crude drugs.

cards.f: Give examples of bush medicines and their modern uses.
cards.b: Tea tree oil (Bundjalung): antiseptic, now for acne and fungi. Eucalyptus oil: decongestants. Kakadu plum: very rich in vitamin C. Emu bush: antibacterial. Kangaroo apple: steroid for cortisone.

cards.f: Smoke bush case study: what was discovered?
cards.b: In the late 1980s the US National Cancer Institute screened WA plants; smoke bush (Conospermum) contained conocurovone, which destroyed HIV at low concentrations in lab tests.

cards.f: Smoke bush case study: why was it an equity problem?
cards.b: AMRAD paid the WA government $1.65 million for rights, but Noongar people received no consent, acknowledgement or royalties. Patents could block their own use of their knowledge (biopiracy).

cards.f: Why is protecting Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) important?
cards.b: It respects original custodians, acknowledges sources, prevents biopiracy, ensures fair benefit-sharing, supports sustainability and keeps knowledge in community control.
Maintaining a relatively stable internal environment within narrow limits despite changes in the external environment.

cards.f: Give the set points for body temperature, blood glucose and blood pH.
cards.b: Temperature about 37 °C; blood glucose about 5 mmol/L; blood pH 7.4.

cards.f: Give the normal ranges for body temperature, blood glucose and blood pH.
cards.b: Temperature about 36.5-37.5 °C; blood glucose about 3.5-8 mmol/L; blood pH 7.35-7.45.
Enzymes work only within narrow temperature and pH ranges; outside them they denature or slow and metabolism fails. Cells also need correct water balance and a steady glucose supply.

cards.f: List the stages of the stimulus-response (negative feedback) model.
cards.b: Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response, then feedback: the variable returns to the set point and the response is switched off.

Negative feedback reverses a change, returning the variable to the set point (homeostatic). Positive feedback amplifies a change to drive a process to completion, e.g. oxytocin in childbirth, blood clotting; not homeostatic.

cards.f: List receptor types and what they detect.
cards.b: Thermoreceptors (temperature), chemoreceptors (CO2, O2, pH, glucose), osmoreceptors (blood solute concentration), nociceptors (damage), mechanoreceptors (pressure, sound), photoreceptors (light).

cards.f: Which part of the brain controls thermoregulation?
cards.b: The hypothalamus: the anterior part mainly coordinates heat loss and the posterior part heat gain and conservation.

cards.f: Where are the thermoreceptors for temperature regulation?
cards.b: Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin (early warning of external change) and central thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus (monitor core blood temperature).

Vasodilation of skin arterioles (more heat lost by radiation), sweating (evaporative cooling), hair erector muscles relax, lower metabolic rate, and behaviour such as seeking shade and removing clothes.
Vasoconstriction, shivering, piloerection (traps insulating air), raised metabolic rate via thyroxine and adrenaline, and behaviour such as adding clothes and huddling.

cards.f: Outline the hormonal pathway that raises metabolic rate in the cold.
cards.b: Hypothalamus releases TRH; anterior pituitary releases TSH; thyroid releases thyroxine (T4) and T3, which raise cellular metabolic rate and heat production.

Endotherms (mammals, birds) generate heat internally by metabolism and keep a fairly constant temperature. Ectotherms (reptiles, fish, amphibians) rely on external heat and regulate by behaviour. The difference is the heat source.

cards.f: Give behavioural thermoregulation adaptations in Australian endotherms.
cards.b: Bilby is nocturnal and burrows; kangaroos lick their forearms (evaporative cooling); mountain pygmy possum hibernates; emperor penguins huddle; grey plover migrates.

cards.f: Give structural thermoregulation adaptations in endotherms.
cards.b: Insulation (fur, feathers, blubber), SA:V ratio (small ears in the Arctic fox, large ears in the fennec fox) and countercurrent heat exchange (penguin feet, dolphin flippers).
Arteries carrying warm blood run beside veins carrying cool blood back; heat transfers to the returning blood and stays in the core, so less is lost from extremities.

cards.f: Give physiological thermoregulation adaptations in endotherms.
cards.b: Sweating, panting (dogs, kangaroos), vasodilation/vasoconstriction, shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis (brown fat), and thyroxine-driven metabolic rate changes.

cards.f: Which cells secrete insulin and glucagon?
cards.b: In the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas: beta cells secrete insulin; alpha cells secrete glucagon.

cards.f: What happens when blood glucose rises?
cards.b: Beta cells release insulin; liver, muscle and fat cells take up more glucose, convert it to glycogen (glycogenesis) and fat, and use more in respiration; blood glucose falls.

cards.f: What happens when blood glucose falls?
cards.b: Alpha cells release glucagon; mainly the liver breaks glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis), makes glucose from amino acids (gluconeogenesis), and fat is broken down; blood glucose rises.

cards.f: What is the main target of glucagon?
cards.b: The liver (and fat cells). Muscle lacks the enzyme to release glucose into the blood, so muscle glycogen only fuels the muscle itself.

cards.f: Which other hormones raise blood glucose?
cards.b: Cortisol (adrenal cortex, long-term stress, drives gluconeogenesis) and adrenaline (adrenal medulla, fight or flight, rapid glycogen breakdown).

Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, no insulin; treated with insulin. Type 2: insulin resistance and/or reduced insulin, linked to obesity and inactivity; managed with diet, exercise, metformin and sometimes insulin.

cards.f: What happens when the body is dehydrated (osmoregulation)?
cards.b: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect high solute concentration; posterior pituitary releases more ADH; collecting ducts insert aquaporins and reabsorb more water; small volume of concentrated urine; thirst is stimulated.

cards.f: What happens after drinking lots of water?
cards.b: Osmoreceptors detect low solute concentration, less ADH is released, collecting ducts become less permeable, and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.

A steroid from the adrenal cortex, released when blood sodium or pressure is low. It increases Na+ reabsorption (and K+ secretion) in the distal tubule and collecting duct; water follows, raising blood volume and pressure.

Chemoreceptors (medulla, carotid and aortic bodies) detect rising CO2 or falling pH; breathing rate and depth increase, kidneys excrete H+ and reabsorb bicarbonate, and blood buffers neutralise acids.
CNS (brain, spinal cord) and PNS. PNS divides into somatic (voluntary, skeletal muscle) and autonomic (involuntary): sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest').

Sympathetic: raises heart rate, dilates pupils, inhibits digestion, raises blood glucose (noradrenaline at nerve endings, adrenaline from adrenal medulla). Parasympathetic: slows heart, stimulates digestion (acetylcholine).

Body (nucleus), Dendrites (carry impulses to the cell body), Axon (away from cell body), Myelin sheath (insulation from Schwann cells, gaps are nodes of Ranvier), Synaptic knobs (release neurotransmitter).
Sensory: receptor to CNS (long dendrites). Interneuron: within the CNS, connects sensory and motor. Motor: CNS to effector (long axon).

cards.f: Describe the resting potential of a neuron.
cards.b: About -70 mV, inside negative. Maintained by the sodium-potassium pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, using ATP) and greater membrane permeability to K+.

cards.f: Describe the stages of an action potential.
cards.b: Threshold about -55 mV (all-or-nothing); depolarisation as Na+ rushes in (to about +35 to +40 mV); repolarisation as K+ leaves; hyperpolarisation to about -80 to -90 mV; refractory period ensures one-way travel.

cards.f: How is an impulse transmitted across a synapse?
cards.b: Impulse reaches the terminal; Ca2+ enters; vesicles release neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) into the cleft; it binds post-synaptic receptors, triggering a new impulse; it is then broken down or reabsorbed.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine (ductless) gland into the blood that acts on target cells with specific receptors.

Steroid (lipid-soluble, e.g. cortisol, aldosterone, oestrogen) cross the membrane and bind receptors inside, affecting gene expression. Peptide (water-soluble, e.g. insulin, ADH) bind membrane receptors and trigger second messengers.

cards.f: Hormones of the anterior and posterior pituitary?
cards.b: Anterior: TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, growth hormone, prolactin. Posterior: releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.

cards.f: Hormones of the adrenal cortex and medulla?
cards.b: Cortex: cortisol (stress, gluconeogenesis) and aldosterone (sodium and water balance). Medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline (fight or flight).
Nervous: electrochemical impulses along neurons, very fast, short-lived, specific targets. Endocrine: hormones in blood, slower, long-lasting, widespread targets. The hypothalamus links both.

cards.f: How do stomata open and close?
cards.b: Guard cells that take in water become turgid and the stoma opens; when they lose water they become flaccid and it closes.

cards.f: What is the role of abscisic acid (ABA)?
cards.b: During water stress ABA causes K+ to leave guard cells; water follows by osmosis, guard cells become flaccid and stomata close, reducing water loss (but also CO2 uptake).
Thick waxy cuticle, few sunken stomata, leaf hairs, rolled leaves (spinifex), small leaves or spines, succulence (cacti), vertical leaves (eucalyptus), deep roots and CAM photosynthesis.
Large flat floating leaves, many stomata on the upper surface, thin or no cuticle, reduced roots and air spaces (aerenchyma) for buoyancy, e.g. water lily.

cards.f: What are the three halophyte salt strategies?
cards.b: Exclusion: roots block salt (grey and red mangroves). Excretion: leaf salt glands secrete salt (grey and river mangroves). Accumulation: salt stored in old leaves that are shed (milky mangrove).
A disease not caused by a pathogen that cannot be transmitted between organisms; caused by genetics, environment, nutrition or lifestyle.

cards.f: What are the categories of non-infectious disease?
cards.b: Genetic, environmental exposure, nutritional, cancer, and degenerative/lifestyle diseases (e.g. cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer's).
Autosomal recessive mutation in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7 (commonly delta F508), producing a faulty chloride ion channel.

cards.f: Symptoms and treatment of cystic fibrosis?
cards.b: Thick sticky mucus in lungs and gut, frequent lung infections, poor digestion, salty sweat, male infertility. Treated with physiotherapy, antibiotics, enzyme supplements, CFTR modulators and lung transplant.

Autosomal recessive mutation in the PAH gene (chromosome 12); no phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine builds up, causing brain damage. Detected by newborn heel-prick test; managed with low-phenylalanine diet.
Autosomal dominant: repeated CAG sequence in the HTT gene (chromosome 4). Progressive brain degeneration, involuntary movements, dementia; onset 30-50 years; no cure.

cards.f: Why do X-linked disorders affect males more?
cards.b: Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed; females usually have a second working X. Examples: haemophilia, red-green colour blindness.
Chromosomes or chromatids fail to separate in meiosis, so gametes have an extra (n+1) or missing (n-1) chromosome, giving trisomy or monosomy after fertilisation.
Trisomy 21 from nondisjunction (about 1 in 800 births, risk rises with maternal age). Intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, poor muscle tone, heart defects.
Patau: trisomy 13 (severe disability, cleft lip, extra fingers, most die in first year). Edwards: trisomy 18 (small head, clenched fists, heart defects, low survival).
Klinefelter: XXY male, tall, low testosterone, infertile. Turner: XO female (monosomy), short, webbed neck, infertile.

cards.f: How does UV radiation cause skin cancer?
cards.b: UV forms thymine dimers in skin cell DNA; unrepaired dimers cause mutations when DNA is copied. Mutations in proto-oncogenes or tumour suppressor genes (p53) cause uncontrolled division and a malignant tumour.
BCC: basal cells, most common, slow, rarely spreads. SCC: squamous cells, faster, can spread. Melanoma: melanocytes, least common but most deadly, metastasises quickly.
About 17,000 new cases a year (54 per 100,000), about 200,000 people living with melanoma, about 1,300 deaths a year (6 per 100,000).

cards.f: Effects of lead and mercury poisoning?
cards.b: Lead (old paint, mining at Broken Hill, Mount Isa): nervous system damage in children, lower IQ, anaemia, kidney damage. Mercury (contaminated fish): tremors, memory loss, birth defects (Minamata disease).
Inhaled fibres lodge in the lungs and pleura, causing chronic inflammation and DNA damage: mesothelioma, asbestosis and lung cancer, 20-50 years after exposure. Banned in Australia in 2003.

Fatty plaques (cholesterol, fat, calcium) build up in artery walls, narrowing them and leading to coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke. Risks: smoking, diet, obesity, hypertension, diabetes.
Tobacco smoke has more than 7,000 chemicals and about 70 carcinogens; it causes about 90% of lung cancers and about 1 in 5 cancer deaths, plus heart disease, stroke and COPD.
Kwashiorkor: severe protein deficiency with some carbohydrate; swollen belly, oedema, hair and skin changes. Marasmus: lack of both protein and energy; severe wasting, 'skin and bones'.
Vitamin A: night blindness. B1 (thiamine): beriberi. C: scurvy (bleeding gums). D: rickets (children) or osteomalacia (adults).
A group of diseases in which cells divide uncontrollably and can invade other tissues, caused by mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle.

Proto-oncogenes stimulate division ('accelerator') and when mutated become oncogenes stuck 'on'. Tumour suppressor genes (p53) stop the cycle and trigger apoptosis ('brakes'); mutation loses this control.

cards.f: What do BRCA1 and BRCA2 do?
cards.b: DNA repair (tumour suppressor) genes; BRCA1 repairs double-strand breaks by homologous recombination. Inherited mutations greatly raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.
Benign: slow, encapsulated, no invasion or spread. Malignant: fast, no capsule, invades tissue and metastasises via blood and lymph.
Carcinoma (epithelial, most common), sarcoma (connective tissue), lymphoma (lymphatic system), leukaemia (blood-forming bone marrow cells).
Chemical (tobacco smoke, asbestos, benzene), physical (UV, X-rays, ionising radiation) and biological (HPV for cervical cancer, hepatitis B for liver cancer).

cards.f: Do non-infectious diseases cause more deaths than infectious diseases?
cards.b: Globally yes: NCDs cause about 74% of deaths (about 41 million a year), mainly CVD, cancer, respiratory disease and diabetes; about 90% in Australia. Infectious diseases remain large in low-income countries.

cards.f: Why do non-infectious diseases dominate deaths?
cards.b: Ageing populations, lifestyle (smoking, diet, inactivity, alcohol), better control of infectious disease by vaccines, antibiotics and sanitation, and the nutrition transition.
The study of the distribution (who, where, when) and determinants (causes, risk factors) of disease in populations, applied to control health problems.

cards.f: Describe the global pattern of obesity.
cards.b: Nearly tripled since 1975; about 13% of adults obese (2016); higher in the Americas (about 26-28%) than SE Asia (3-5%); higher in women. Overweight 5-19-year-olds rose from about 4% to 18%.
Countries such as India and China moving from traditional diets to Western diets high in processed food, sugar and fat, with urbanisation and less activity, increasing obesity.
They describe disease patterns by person, place and time to generate hypotheses. Cheap and quick but cannot show cause and effect.
Retrospective: compares people with the disease to those without and looks back at exposure, e.g. Doll and Hill 1947-50 (about 2,475 patients). Quick, cheap, good for rare diseases; but recall bias.
Prospective: follows healthy exposed and unexposed people over time, e.g. British Doctors Study (1951, about 40,000 doctors, ran 50 years). Measures incidence and sequence; expensive, slow, dropouts.

cards.f: What is a randomised controlled trial?
cards.b: Participants randomly assigned to treatment or placebo control, often double-blind. The gold standard because randomisation reduces bias; expensive and can raise ethical issues.

cards.f: Criteria for a valid epidemiological study?
cards.b: Large random representative sample, control group, one independent variable, randomisation and blinding, long duration, repeatable results, peer review, ethics approval and informed consent.
A third variable linked to both exposure and disease, creating a false association, e.g. coffee drinkers get more lung cancer because more of them smoke.
A prospective cohort of about 1,728 Pima people (Gila River, Arizona, USA), 1987-2000. Higher physical activity was linked to lower type 2 diabetes incidence, even adjusting for BMI.

cards.f: What did comparing Arizona and Mexican Pima show?
cards.b: Mexican Pima with an active farming lifestyle have much lower diabetes rates despite similar genes, showing lifestyle plays a big role.

Strengths: large sample, 13 years, prospective, objective glucose tests, adjusted for BMI and age. Weaknesses: self-reported activity, one high-risk population, confounders (diet, genes), loss to follow-up.

cards.f: What did 1970s US smoking data show?
cards.b: Among about 1 million men, lung cancer deaths were far higher in smokers and rose with cigarettes smoked (dose-response). Female rates rose 20-30 years after male rates because women started smoking later.
Leading cause of cancer death: about 12,700 new cases and 9,000 deaths a year. Risk factors: smoking, radiotherapy, asbestos and air pollution.
Identify causes (smoking, UV, asbestos), lead to campaigns and laws (QUIT, SunSmart, plain packaging), evaluate programs, inform screening, plan services, predict trends and identify at-risk groups.
They show association, not always causation; are expensive and slow; have ethical limits; and are affected by bias and confounding.

Surgery removes localised tumours. Chemotherapy kills rapidly dividing cells body-wide (hair loss, nausea). Radiotherapy damages cancer cell DNA locally. Targeted therapy (BRAF inhibitors) and immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T) use specific mechanisms.
Diet and exercise, metformin, insulin injections or pumps, artificial pancreas (glucose monitor linked to pump), islet transplants; future: stem-cell beta cells and gene therapy.

cards.f: Features of a successful health campaign?
cards.b: Clear memorable message, targeted at risk groups, many media, emotive imagery, backed by legislation and taxes, sustained and updated, evaluated with data, support services, culturally appropriate.

cards.f: Key Australian tobacco control measures and years?
cards.b: 1993 advertising ban; 1997 National Tobacco Campaign; 2006 graphic warnings; 2010 25% excise rise; 2012 world-first plain packaging; 2013-2020 12.5% yearly excise rises; 2024 vapes pharmacy-only.

cards.f: How effective has the QUIT campaign been?
cards.b: Smoking fell from about 24% (early 1990s) to about 8.3% daily smokers (2022-23); male lung cancer fell since the 1980s; about 55,000 lives saved. Limits: vaping, inequality, illegal tobacco.
Cancer Council campaign launched in Victoria in 1981: 'Slip, Slop, Slap' (Sid the Seagull), later 'Seek, Slide'. Uses ads, 'No hat, no play', UV alerts, shade and the 2015 solarium ban.

Melanoma in under-40s fell from about 25 to 14 per 100,000 (1996-2010); about 43,000 skin cancers prevented in Victoria; very cost-effective. Limits: high rates in older people, inconsistent use, vitamin D concerns.
IVF embryos grow to blastocyst (about day 5); a few cells are biopsied and tested (PCR for single-gene disorders, aCGH or sequencing for aneuploidy); only unaffected embryos are implanted.
Advantages: prevents passing on serious genetic disease, reduces miscarriage. Disadvantages: expensive, ethical concerns (designer babies, destroying embryos), not 100% accurate.

cards.f: How is the HPV vaccine made and why is it effective?
cards.b: The HPV L1 capsid gene is inserted into yeast or insect cells; the protein self-assembles into virus-like particles with no viral DNA. Developed by Ian Frazer; given at 12-13; prevents cervical cancer.

Rice engineered with daffodil/maize and bacterial genes to make beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor) to prevent vitamin A deficiency blindness. Approved in the Philippines in 2021; concerns about GM, cost, dietary fat.

cards.f: Five steps for developing a prevention strategy?
cards.b: 1. Identify the disease and at-risk group. 2. Identify risk factors. 3. Design the strategy with clear goals. 4. Implement in a culturally appropriate way. 5. Evaluate with data and modify.

cards.f: Functions of the outer ear structures?
cards.b: Pinna collects and funnels sound; auditory canal directs it to the eardrum (wax and hairs protect); the tympanic membrane vibrates at the sound's frequency.
The malleus, incus and stapes transmit and amplify vibrations (about 20 times) from the eardrum to the oval window.

cards.f: What do the round window and vestibular apparatus do?
cards.b: The round window bulges out to release cochlear fluid pressure (not part of transmission). The vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals) controls balance and is not part of the cochlea.

cards.f: Describe the pathway of sound through the ear.
cards.b: Pinna, ear canal, eardrum vibrates, ossicles amplify, stapes pushes oval window, cochlear fluid waves, basilar membrane vibrates, hair cells bend against tectorial membrane, auditory nerve carries impulses to the auditory cortex.

cards.f: How is pitch detected in the cochlea?
cards.b: High frequencies vibrate the narrow, stiff base of the basilar membrane; low frequencies vibrate the wide, flexible apex. Humans hear about 20-20,000 Hz.
Sound cannot pass through the outer or middle ear: wax, otitis media (common in Aboriginal children), perforated eardrum, otosclerosis, glue ear. Usually correctable medically or surgically.

Damage to cochlear hair cells or the auditory nerve: ageing (presbycusis), noise, genetics (GJB2/connexin 26), rubella, meningitis, ototoxic drugs. Often not correctable; hearing aids or cochlear implants used.

cards.f: What are auditory processing disorder and tinnitus?
cards.b: APD: ears work but the brain struggles to interpret sound. Tinnitus: ringing with no external sound, often from noise-damaged hair cells; the most common hearing disorder.

cards.f: How does a hearing aid work and who is it for?
cards.b: Microphone picks up sound, amplifier strengthens it, receiver/speaker delivers louder sound into the canal. For mild to severe loss; needs working eardrum, ossicles and partly functional cochlea.
Advantages: non-invasive, cheap (subsidised), adjustable, discreet. Disadvantages: only amplifies, amplifies background noise, feedback, batteries, discomfort, useless for profound loss.

cards.f: How does a bone conduction implant work?
cards.b: A titanium implant fuses with the skull behind the ear; a processor turns sound into vibrations that travel through bone to the cochlea, bypassing outer and middle ear. A softband version suits young children.

For conductive or mixed loss and single-sided deafness. Advantages: bypasses damaged outer/middle ear, clearer sound, ear canal open. Disadvantages: surgery and infection risk, cost, needs a working cochlea.

cards.f: How does a cochlear implant work?
cards.b: Microphone picks up sound; speech processor digitises it; transmitter coil sends it through skin to an implanted receiver; up to 22 electrodes in the cochlea stimulate the auditory nerve, bypassing damaged hair cells.

Highly effective for severe-profound sensorineural loss, especially early in children; over 1 million users. Limits: major surgery, $30,000-50,000+, unnatural sound needing training, destroys residual hearing, needs working auditory nerve.

cards.f: Roles of the cornea and lens?
cards.b: The cornea refracts most light (about 2/3 of focusing power). The lens fine-focuses light onto the retina by changing shape (accommodation).

cards.f: Roles of the iris and pupil?
cards.b: The muscular iris controls pupil size: it constricts in bright light to protect photoreceptors and dilates in dim light.

cards.f: Roles of the aqueous and vitreous humour?
cards.b: Aqueous humour (between cornea and lens) maintains shape and nourishes cornea and lens. Vitreous humour (jelly) fills the main chamber and maintains eye shape.

cards.f: What are the retina, fovea and blind spot?
cards.b: Retina: light-sensitive layer of rods and cones. Fovea: most cones, sharpest colour vision. Blind spot: where the optic nerve leaves; no photoreceptors.
Rods: about 125 million, dim light, night and peripheral vision, black and white, rhodopsin. Cones: about 6 million, bright light and colour (red, green, blue), concentrated in the fovea.
Light changes the shape of retinal (from vitamin A), which separates from opsin, triggering reactions that create nerve impulses in the optic nerve.

cards.f: Describe accommodation for near and distant objects.
cards.b: Near: ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes rounder and refracts more. Distant: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tighten, lens flattens and refracts less.

cards.f: What is myopia and how is it corrected?
cards.b: Short-sightedness: eyeball too long or cornea too curved, so distant light focuses in front of the retina. Corrected with a concave (diverging) lens or LASIK to flatten the cornea.

cards.f: What is hyperopia and how is it corrected?
cards.b: Long-sightedness: eyeball too short or cornea too flat, so near light focuses behind the retina. Corrected with a convex (converging) lens or LASIK to steepen the cornea.
Presbyopia: the lens stiffens with age (over 40) so near focus fails; reading glasses. Astigmatism: irregular cornea or lens blurs vision at all distances; cylindrical (toric) lenses or laser.
Crystallin proteins in the lens clump, making it cloudy (ageing, UV, diabetes, smoking); blurry vision and glare; leading cause of blindness worldwide. Treated by cataract surgery.

Age-related damage to the macula causing loss of central vision; the leading cause of blindness in Australia. Dry form: gradual. Wet form: leaking vessels, sudden loss, treated with anti-VEGF injections.

cards.f: What are colour blindness and glaucoma?
cards.b: Colour blindness: usually X-linked faulty cones (red-green in about 8% of males). Glaucoma: raised pressure from poor aqueous drainage damages the optic nerve, losing peripheral vision.
Non-invasive, cheap, safe and effective, but only correct, do not cure; glasses can be lost or broken; contacts risk eye infection and dry eyes.

Anaesthetic drops; a corneal flap is cut and folded back; an excimer laser vaporises corneal tissue (flattening for myopia, steepening for hyperopia); the flap is replaced and heals without stitches. The lens is not changed.

Advantages: permanent, quick (about 15 min), fast recovery, over 95% success. Disadvantages: $2,000-3,000 per eye, dry eyes, halos, infection; must be 18+ with stable prescription; doesn't prevent presbyopia.

Phacoemulsification: a small corneal incision; ultrasound breaks up the cloudy lens; fragments are suctioned out; a foldable intraocular lens is inserted. Over 95% success, but the IOL cannot accommodate.
Excretes urea and toxins; osmoregulation; salt and pH balance; blood pressure control; hormones (EPO, renin, activates vitamin D).

cards.f: What is the nephron and where are its parts?
cards.b: The kidney's functional unit (about 1 million per kidney). Glomeruli, Bowman's capsules and convoluted tubules are in the cortex; loops of Henle and collecting ducts in the medulla.

cards.f: Describe the four steps of urine formation.
cards.b: 1. Filtration: high pressure forces small molecules from glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. 2. Reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, water, salts (mainly PCT). 3. Secretion of H+, K+, drugs (DCT). 4. Excretion of urine.

cards.f: Roles of the loop of Henle, DCT and collecting duct?
cards.b: Loop of Henle: creates a salt gradient for water reabsorption. DCT: fine-tunes salt and pH; aldosterone acts here. Collecting duct: water reabsorption controlled by ADH.

cards.f: What are the main causes of kidney failure?
cards.b: Diabetes (leading cause), high blood pressure, glomerulonephritis (common cause), smoking, lupus, polycystic kidney disease, infection, kidney stones, drugs and ageing.

cards.f: Why is kidney disease called a 'silent disease'?
cards.b: Up to 90% of function can be lost before symptoms (fatigue, oedema, urine changes, nausea, itching, anaemia) appear.
When kidneys work at less than about 10-15% capacity, so dialysis or a transplant is needed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are about 4-5 times more likely to have it.

Blood from a fistula is pumped through hollow selectively permeable fibres; dialysate flows countercurrent with no urea and normal glucose and salts, so urea diffuses out; ultrafiltration removes water; heparin prevents clotting.
About 2 L of dialysate enters the abdomen by catheter; the peritoneum acts as the membrane; wastes diffuse in over a 4-6 hour dwell; fluid is drained and replaced, about 4 times daily or overnight.
Haemodialysis: artificial membrane, clinic or home, 3-4 sessions a week, needles, strict diet. Peritoneal: own peritoneum, at home daily, more independence, no needles, but peritonitis risk.

cards.f: Compare dialysis with a normal kidney.
cards.b: Kidney: continuous, selective reabsorption and secretion, makes hormones, fine ADH and aldosterone control. Dialysis: intermittent, passive diffusion only, no hormones, about 10-15% of normal function.

Life-saving and keeps patients alive awaiting transplant, but not a cure; time-consuming, about $80,000+ a year, reduced quality of life, strict diet, infection risk, shorter life expectancy than transplant.

cards.f: How is rejection of a kidney transplant reduced?
cards.b: Matching blood group and MHC/HLA markers, cross-matching for existing antibodies, and lifelong immunosuppressants (which raise infection and cancer risk).

Best treatment: near-normal function including hormones, better quality and length of life, cheaper long-term. But major surgery, lifelong immunosuppressants, rejection risk, donor shortage (2-4 year wait), lasts 10-20 years.

cards.f: Roles of FSH and LH in the menstrual cycle?
cards.b: FSH (anterior pituitary) stimulates follicle growth and oestrogen production. An LH surge triggers ovulation (about day 14) and converts the empty follicle into the corpus luteum.
Oestrogen thickens the endometrium and at high levels triggers the LH surge. Progesterone (corpus luteum, later placenta) maintains the endometrium and inhibits FSH and LH.

cards.f: What happens if no fertilisation occurs?
cards.b: The corpus luteum degenerates (days 24-28), progesterone and oestrogen fall, the endometrium is shed (menstruation), and FSH rises again.

cards.f: What is the role of hCG?
cards.b: Secreted by the embryo's chorion after implantation; maintains the corpus luteum so progesterone stays high. Detected by pregnancy tests; after about 8-10 weeks the placenta takes over.

cards.f: Why is childbirth an example of positive feedback?
cards.b: The baby presses on the cervix; stretch receptors signal the hypothalamus; the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, causing stronger contractions and more oxytocin until birth ends the loop.
